Klein’s ten planar dessins of degree 1111,
and beyond

Gareth A. Jones    Alexander K. Zvonkin
Abstract

We reinterpret ideas in Klein’s paper on transformations of degree 1111 from the modern point of view of dessins d’enfants, and extend his results by considering dessins of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) and degree pp or p+1p+1, where pp is prime. In many cases we determine the passports and monodromy groups of these dessins, and in a few small cases we give drawings which are topologically (or, in certain examples, even geometrically) correct. We use the Bateman–Horn Conjecture and extensive computer searches to support a conjecture that there are infinitely many primes of the form p=(qn−1)/(q−1)p=(q^{n}-1)/(q-1) for some prime power qq, in which case infinitely many groups PSLn​(q){\rm PSL}_{n}(q) arise as permutation groups and monodromy groups of degree pp (an open problem in group theory).

2010 Mathematics Subject Classification. Primary 14H57, secondary 05C10, 11G32, 11N13, 11N32, 20B20, 20B25.

Key words and phrases. Plane tree, dessin d’enfant, map, monodromy group, projective groups of prime degree, groups containing a cycle, dessins on elliptic curves, Belyĭ functions, Bateman–Horn Conjecture.

1 Introduction

In 1878–9 Klein published two papers [50, 51] with almost identical titles. The first concerned equations of degree 77, while the second concerned those of degree 1111, with the properties and actions of the groups PSL2​(p){\rm PSL}_{2}(p), for p=7p=7 and 1111 respectively, playing a major role in them. The paper [50] is deservedly famous, not least for introducing the Hauptfigur, the iconic diagram of a tessellation of a hyperbolic 1414-gon which, after identification of sides, yields the quartic curve of genus 33 now named after Klein: see [55], a book entirely devoted to this curve. In contrast with the largely geometric approach taken in [50], Klein’s emphasis in [51] was more algebraic. However, that paper contained a diagram11 1 Regrettably this diagram, like that of the Hauptfigur in [50], is omitted from the on-line version of the paper, both having been provided on separate inserted sheets in the original journal. However, both diagrams can be found in Klein’s collected works [53, vol. 3, pp. 126, 143], integrated into updated versions of the two papers; see also [55, pp. 115, 320] for the Hauptfigur. showing ten plane trees, which anticipated Grothendieck’s concept of dessins d’enfants [35] by over a century. Our aim here is to reinterpret this diagram and the mathematics underlying it from a modern point of view, and to explore some generalisations which Klein might have been able to achieve if he had had access to such tools as character theory, computer algebra and the classification of finite simple groups.

In particular, we study dessins of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) and of degree pp or p+1p+1 for arbitrary primes pp, extending Klein’s work in [51] on the case p=11p=11. These dessins are best studied through their monodromy groups, which are permutation groups of these degrees, and in principle such groups are all known, as a consequence of the classification of finite simple groups. However, because of certain open problems in number theory it is unknown whether two families of these groups, consisting of projective and affine groups of degrees pp and p+1p+1, are finite or infinite. Using the Bateman–Horn Conjecture and extensive computer searches, we present what we believe is strong evidence that the first of these two families is infinite. (The second family is based on the Mersenne primes, and we have nothing new to add about its cardinality.)

In Section 2 we describe Klein’s ten plane trees, firstly as he presented them in [51], as pictorial representions of the possible 11-sheeted coverings of the Riemann sphere Σ=ℙ1​(ℂ)\Sigma={\mathbb{P}}^{1}({\mathbb{C}}) with branching patterns 33​123^{3}1^{2}, 24​132^{4}1^{3} and 11111^{1} over 00, 11 and ∞\infty. We then use more modern terminology and graphic conventions to describe them as dessins d’enfants, specifically as bipartite maps (Figure 2) and as maps with free edges (Figure 3). Klein asserted without proof that his list was complete, so we outline a method he might have used to see this.

An important invariant of any dessin is its monodromy group (equivalently the monodromy group of the covering of the sphere which it represents), discussed in Section 3. This is a transitive permutation group on the sheets of the covering (more precisely, on the fibre over a base-point), generated by the monodromy permutations describing the branching over the critical values. Klein showed that just one chiral pair of his trees, corresponding to our maps ℳ1{\mathcal{M}}_{1} and ℳ¯1\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1}, have monodromy groups isomorphic to PSL2​(11){\rm PSL}_{2}(11), acting with degree 1111; we show that the other eight have the alternating group A11{\rm A}_{11} as their monodromy group.

A powerful technique for enumerating dessins with a given monodromy group, but unavailable to Klein when he wrote his papers, is the character-theoretic triple-counting formula introduced by Frobenius [25] in 1896. We use this in Section 4, with the aid of character tables provided by GAP [28] and by the ATLAS [17], to confirm Klein’s enumeration of the trees and our description of their monodromy groups; this includes the elimination of the Mathieu group M11{\rm M}_{11}, another possible candidate.

Any dessin 𝒟\mathcal{D} with monodromy group GG has a unique minimal regular cover, a regular dessin ℛ\mathcal{R} with Aut​ℛ≅G{\rm Aut}\,{\mathcal{R}}\cong G. Much of Klein’s paper [51] is devoted to the common regular cover ℛ1{\mathcal{R}}_{1} of ℳ1{\mathcal{M}}_{1} and ℳ¯1\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1}, a map on the modular curve X⁡(11)X(11) of genus 2626. We show in Section 5 that the other eight trees, with G≅A11G\cong{\rm A}_{11}, have mutually non-isomorphic regular covers of genus 756 001756\,001.

Each of Klein’s ten trees corresponds to an 1111-sheeted covering Σ→Σ\Sigma\to\Sigma realised by a Shabat polynomial PP of degree 1111. In Section 6 we determine these polynomials for ℳ1{\mathcal{M}}_{1} and ℳ¯1\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1}: they are defined over ℚ⁡(−11){\mathbb{Q}}(\sqrt{-11}), and are transposed by the Galois group of that field, while those for the other eight trees form a single Galois orbit. Whereas the illustrations of dessins given so far are only topologically correct, we compute and show in Figure 8 a geometrically correct drawing of ℳ1{\mathcal{M}}_{1} as the inverse image under PP of the unit interval.

In Section 7 we extend Klein’s classification by determining all the dessins of degree 1111 and type (3,2,r)(3,2,r) for r≠11r\neq 11: there are sixteen of them (see Figure 9), all of genus 00 and with the symmetric group S11{\rm S}_{11} as their monodromy group.

In Sections 8, 9 and 10 we generalise Klein’s work further by considering dessins 𝒟\mathcal{D} of degree pp and type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) for arbitrary primes pp. The investigation is quite difficult, because we encounter some important open problems in group theory and number theory. The monodromy group GG of 𝒟\mathcal{D} must be a transitive permutation group of degree pp, and if p>3p>3 (as we shall assume) then as a quotient of the triangle group Δ⁡(3,2,p)\Delta(3,2,p) with mutually coprime periods, GG must be perfect. In Section 8 we use the classification of finite simple groups, and hence of permutation groups of prime degree, to restrict the possibilities for GG to the alternating groups Ap{\rm A}_{p}, PSL2​(11){\rm PSL}_{2}(11) and the Mathieu groups M11{\rm M}_{11} and M23{\rm M}_{23} for p=11p=11, 1111 and 2323, and PSLn​(q){\rm PSL}_{n}(q) in cases where its natural degree (qn−1)/(q−1)(q^{n}-1)/(q-1) is a prime pp. We show that Ap{\rm A}_{p} arises for p=5p=5 and each p≥11p\geq 11, with exponentially many dessins (far too many to classify) as p→∞p\to\infty. The group PSL2​(11){\rm PSL}_{2}(11), acting with degree 1111, was dealt with by Klein, as we have already seen, while the Frobenius triple-counting formula eliminates the Mathieu groups as quotients of Δ⁡(3,2,p)\Delta(3,2,p).

This leaves the groups PSLn​(q){\rm PSL}_{n}(q), acting naturally with degree (qn−1)/(q−1)(q^{n}-1)/(q-1) for some prime power qq. In Section 9 we consider the open problem of whether this degree is prime for finitely or infinitely many pairs (n,q)(n,q); such projective primes, as we call them, include the Fermat and Mersenne primes, for n=2n=2 and q=2q=2 respectively. For each n≥3n\geq 3 (necessarily prime) the Bateman–Horn Conjecture (a powerful but apparently little-known open problem in number theory) provides a heuristic estimate for the number of primes t≤xt\leq x such that q=teq=t^{e} and (qn−1)/(q−1)(q^{n}-1)/(q-1) is prime; since these estimates agree closely with results obtained from computer searches revealing large numbers of examples, we conjecture that for each prime n≥3n\geq 3 there are infinitely many projective primes pp. This case is explored in more detail in [46].

In Section 10 we return to the dessins of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) and degree pp for projective primes p=(qn−1)/(q−1)p=(q^{n}-1)/(q-1). Using character theory we show that in the cases n=2n=2 and 33 there are such dessins with monodromy group PSLn​(q){\rm PSL}_{n}(q) for each projective prime pp; in Theorems 10.1 and 10.3 we enumerate them and give their genus. Theorem 10.11 is a similar but weaker result for q=2q=2, proving the existence of such dessins for each Mersenne prime p=2n−1p=2^{n}-1, and we conjecture that it extends to all projective primes.

In Sections 11 and 12 we consider dessins of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) and degree p+1p+1 for arbitrary primes pp. The parameters 33 and 22 in the types of the dessins we have considered imply that all the monodromy groups and automorphism groups associated with them are quotients of the modular group PSL2​(ℤ)≅C3∗C2{\rm PSL}_{2}({\mathbb{Z}})\cong{\rm C}_{3}*{\rm C}_{2}. In most cases the corresponding kernels are non-congruence subgroups, but in Section 11 we consider the modular dessins 𝒟0​(p){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(p) arising from reduction of coefficients mod (p)(p), corresponding to the action of PSL2​(p){\rm PSL}_{2}(p) on the projective line ℙ1​(𝔽p){\mathbb{P}}^{1}({\mathbb{F}}_{p}). We do this firstly in the planar cases p≤7p\leq 7 and p=13p=13, and then in the more difficult case p=11p=11, where we outline a calculation by John Voight which determines both the underlying elliptic curve EE and the Belyĭ function E→ΣE\to\Sigma. For p=11p=11 and 1313 we compute and display geometrically correct drawings of these dessins.

We extend this further in Section 12 by considering arbitrary dessins of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) and degree p+1p+1 for primes p>3p>3. We use the classification by Müller [65] of primitive permutation groups containing a cycle with one fixed point to restrict the possible monodromy groups to Ap+1{\rm A}_{p+1}, PSL2​(p){\rm PSL}_{2}(p), AGLn​(2){\rm AGL}_{n}(2) for p=2n−1p=2^{n}-1, M11{\rm M}_{11} and M12{\rm M}_{12} for p=11p=11, and M24{\rm M}_{24} for p=23p=23. We show that Ap+1{\rm A}_{p+1} arises for all p>7p>7, again with too many dessins to classify for all except small pp, whereas PSL2​(p){\rm PSL}_{2}(p) arises only for 𝒟0​(p){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(p). The Mathieu groups M12{\rm M}_{12} and M24{\rm M}_{24} each yield two chiral pairs of dessins, whereas as before M11{\rm M}_{11} yields none. Finally we show that the affine group AGLn​(2){\rm AGL}_{n}(2) yields at least one dessin for each Mersenne prime p=2n−1>7p=2^{n}-1>7; however, this fails for p=7p=7 since AGL3​(2){\rm AGL}_{3}(2) is not a Hurwitz group.

In Section 13 we briefly outline another realisation of PSL2​(11){\rm PSL}_{2}(11), this time as the isometry group of the hendecachoron, a tessellation of a non-orientable 33-orbifold by 1111 hemi-icosahedra, discovered independently by Grünbaum [36] and Coxeter [18].

Section 14 contains monodromy permutations and diagrams for some of the dessins which appear in this paper.

2 Klein’s ten plane trees

In [51] Klein drew a diagram showing ten plane trees, each with eleven edges and twelve vertices. In each tree there is a bipartite partition of the vertices, with five vertices (coloured white) of valencies dividing 33, and seven vertices (indicated by short cross-bars, perpendicular to their incident edges) of valencies dividing 22; in each case the unique face is an 1111-gon. Among these plane trees there are four chiral (mirror-image) pairs, numbered I to IV, and two others, numbered V and VI, which exhibit bilateral symmetry. The chiral pair I, which play a major role in Klein’s paper, are shown (slightly distorted for simplicity, but combinatorially correct) in Figure 1.

2.1 Klein’s trees as dessins d’enfants

If we regard the underlying surface as the complex plane ℂ{\mathbb{C}}, and compactify it to give the Riemann sphere or complex projective line Σ=ℙ1​(ℂ)=ℂ∪{∞}\Sigma={\mathbb{P}}^{1}({\mathbb{C}})={\mathbb{C}}\cup\{\infty\}, we can recognise these plane trees as dessins d’enfants in Grothendieck’s sense [35], namely bipartite graphs embedded in compact Riemann surfaces XX; as such they represent finite covers X→ΣX\to\Sigma of the sphere, unbranched outside {0,1,∞}\{0,1,\infty\}, or equivalently, by Belyĭ’s Theorem [6], projective algebraic curves XX defined over algebraic number fields. (See [30, 44, 54] for background on dessins d’enfants.) All ten of these dessins have genus 00, so that X=ΣX=\Sigma. They have degree 1111, meaning that they represent 1111-sheeted coverings of Σ\Sigma; they have type (3,2,11)(3,2,11), meaning that there are branch-points of orders dividing 3,23,2 and 1111 over 0,10,1 and ∞\infty, represented in Klein’s diagrams by the white vertices, cross-bars and the point at infinity. A modern convention is to use black and white vertices for points over 00 and 11, with the edges corresponding to the points over the unit interval [0,1]⊂Σ[0,1]\subset\Sigma, and to regard those over ∞\infty as the face-centres. We will denote the dessins corresponding to Klein’s chiral pairs I to IV by ℳi{\mathcal{M}}_{i} and ℳ¯i\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{i} for i=1,…,4i=1,\ldots,4, with ℳi{\mathcal{M}}_{i} on the left in Klein’s diagrams and ours; similarly ℳi​(i=5,6){\mathcal{M}}_{i}\;(i=5,6) is the dessin corresponding to the tree V or VI in [51]22 2 The temptation to follow Klein by using Roman numerals as subscripts here was almost (but not totally) irresistible.. The dessins ℳ1{\mathcal{M}}_{1} and ℳ¯1\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1} corresponding to Klein’s plane trees I are shown in Figure 2.

When the order of branching over 11 divides 22, as in these dessins, so that white vertices all have valencies 11 or 22, it is sometimes convenient to omit these vertices, leaving a map with only black vertices and possibly some free edges where white vertices of valency 11 have been removed. Of course, this operation is reversible, so no information is lost. With this convention, the dessins corresponding to all ten of Klein’s plane trees are shown in Figure 3, with the same layout as in his original diagram.

In fact these ten dessins form a complete list (up to isomorphism) of the dessins of type (3,2,11)(3,2,11) and degree 1111, which is the least possible degree for dessins of this type. Klein presented his diagram as representing a classification of the 1111-sheeted coverings of the sphere Σ\Sigma with branching patterns 33​123^{3}1^{2} and 24​132^{4}1^{3} over 00 and 11. He explained this in terms of the modular function J:ℍ→ΣJ:{\mathbb{H}}\to\Sigma, which parametrises isomorphism classes of elliptic curves, an approach which leads naturally to the modular group Γ=PSL2​(ℤ)\Gamma={\rm PSL}_{2}({\mathbb{Z}}), the subgroup leaving JJ invariant in the automorphism group PSL2​(ℝ){\rm PSL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}}) of the Riemann surface ℍ\mathbb{H}. This part of Klein’s work will not be discussed in our paper.

2.2 The classification problem

Klein presented his ten planar trees in [51, §1] in answer to a question he had posed in [49, §5]: in modern terminology, he had asked for the number of dessins 𝒟\mathcal{D} of degree 1111 and passport (3312;2413;−)(3^{3}1^{2};2^{4}1^{3};-), that is, with three black vertices of valency 33 and two of valency 11, together with four white vertices of valency 22 and three of valency 11, and with no restrictions on the faces.

In his diagram Klein drew ten planar trees, equivalent to these dessins, but did not explain why this list was complete, writing simply ‘Dass es auch nicht mehr giebt, ist ebenso evident’33 3 ‘It is also clear that there are no others.’. The argument, which we will now give in the language of dessins, is indeed straightforward. Since each dessin 𝒟\mathcal{D} has eleven edges and twelve vertices the embedded graph, being connected, must be a tree, so the underlying surface is the sphere and there is a single face, of valency 1111. Since the white vertices have valency 11 or 22 we can omit them and for simplicity represent 𝒟\mathcal{D} as a map ℳ\mathcal{M}, which must have three vertices of valency 33 and two of valency 11, and seven edges, three of them free. By connectedness, one of the three vertices of valency 33 must be adjacent to the other two, so ℳ\mathcal{M} must be formed from the basic map ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0} in Figure 4 by choosing two of its five free edges and adding a vertex to each. This gives us (52)=10\displaystyle\left(\!\!\begin{array}[]{c}5\\ 2\end{array}\!\!\right)=10 non-isomorphic maps ℳ\mathcal{M}; they are shown in Figure 3, with the same layout as the corresponding plane trees in Klein’s paper [51].

An alternative approach to this and similar problems, based on the character theory and the Frobenius formula, will be developed in Section 4.

3 Monodromy groups

Any dessin 𝒟\mathcal{D} of degree nn can be represented as an ordered pair x,yx,y of permutations of its nn edges, obtained by using the chosen orientation of the underlying surface to follow the rotation of edges around their incident black and white vertices. The monodromy group G=⟨x,y⟩G=\langle x,y\rangle of 𝒟\mathcal{D}, through its action permuting the nn edges, can be identified with a subgroup of the symmetric group Sn{\rm S}_{n}. By the connectedness of the embedded graph it is transitive. It is convenient to introduce a third permutation z:=(x​y)−1z:=(xy)^{-1}, so that x​y​z=1xyz=1. It is easy to verify that, while the cycles of xx and yy correspond respectively to black and white vertices, the cycles of zz correspond to faces.

Convention 3.1 (Where to put labels)

We put a label of an edge on its left side while moving from its black end to its white one. In this way the labels corresponding to a cycle of zz or, equivalently, to a face, will be situated inside this face and will be rotated by zz around the center of the face in the direction corresponding to the orientation of the surface. This convention is illustrated in Figure 5.

(When a dessin is drawn on the plane, its outer face gives an impression that its labels are rotated in the direction opposite to the orientation of the plane. But this is an illusion. In fact, the dessin should be considered not on the plane but on a sphere, and the center of the outer face is situated on the “opposite side” of this sphere. Looking from this center, the rotation of the labels of the outer face does correspond to the orientation of the sphere.)

When y2=1y^{2}=1 and the white vertices are omitted, so that 𝒟\mathcal{D} is a map, one can regard GG as permuting its half-edges, or else directed edges. Thus, an edge of a map bears two labels while a free edge bears only one. A free edge may be considered as an outgoing directed edge.

The permutations corresponding to the map in Figure 6 are as follows:

The ten dessins 𝒟\mathcal{D} considered here have degree 1111, so their monodromy groups GG are transitive subgroups of S11{\rm S}_{11}. In each case x3=y2=1x^{3}=y^{2}=1, so GG is a quotient of the modular group

(Here we have associated Möbius transformations t↦a​t+bc​t+d\displaystyle t\mapsto\frac{at+b}{ct+d} with pairs of matrices ±(acbd)\displaystyle\pm\,\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}a&c\\ b&d\end{array}\right), the transposes of those normally used in this context. This is because we will later need to regard Möbius transformations, especially those over finite fields, as permutations; it is algebraically and computationally convenient to compose these from left to right, instead of using the analytic right to left convention, so in order to have a homomorphism from matrices to Möbius transformations we will ignore the deceptively suggestive notation for the latter and use transposes.)

Klein was interested in which of these monodromy groups GG are congruence quotients, that is, which are quotients by congruence subgroups of Γ\Gamma. The only possible level for such a congruence subgroup is 1111 (since this is the order of z:=(x​y)−1z:=(xy)^{-1}), and indeed the resulting quotient group L:=PSL2​(11)L:={\rm PSL}_{2}(11), a simple group of order 660660, does act as a transitive group of degree 1111, namely on the cosets of a subgroup H≅A5H\cong{\rm A}_{5}, as we will now show. This is one of the three cases, all known to Galois (see [27], pp. 411–412), in which a simple group PSL2​(p){\rm PSL}_{2}(p), where pp is prime, has a proper subgroup of index less than p+1p+1; the others are A4<PSL2​(5){\rm A}_{4}<{\rm PSL}_{2}(5) and S4<PSL2​(7){\rm S}_{4}<{\rm PSL}_{2}(7).

induces an outer automorphism of LL, transposing u,vu,v and ww with elements

u¯=±(41−2−3),v¯=v=y=±(0−110),w¯=±(2431)\overline{u}=\pm\left(\,\begin{array}[]{cc}4&1\\ -2&-3\\ \end{array}\right),\quad\overline{v}=v=y=\pm\left(\,\begin{array}[]{cc}0&-1\\ 1&0\\ \end{array}\right),\quad\overline{w}=\pm\left(\,\begin{array}[]{cc}2&4\\ 3&1\\ \end{array}\right)

which satisfy the same relations and therefore generate a subgroup H¯≅A5\overline{H}\cong{\rm A}_{5}. This subgroup is not conjugate in LL to HH: if it were, some non-identity element of PGL2​(11){\rm PGL}_{2}(11) would commute with u,vu,v and ww, whereas it is straightforward to check that only the identity element does this. It follows that LL has two inequivalent transitive representations of degree 1111, on the cosets of the subgroups HH and H¯\overline{H}, or equivalently (since these subgroups are equal to their normalisers in LL), by conjugation on the two conjugacy classes of subgroups they represent.

Nowadays, by using a program such as GAP [28] one can easily determine the monodromy groups of the ten dessins, showing that those with monodromy group L=PSL2​(11)L={\rm PSL}_{2}(11) are the chiral pair ℳ1\mathcal{M}_{1} and ℳ¯1\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1}. However, one can also distinguish this pair by hand: for i=1,…,6i=1,\ldots,6 the commutator [x,y]=x−1​y−1​x​y[x,y]=x^{-1}y^{-1}xy has cycle structure 52​11,71​31​11,81​21​11,51​41​21,71​225^{2}1^{1},7^{1}3^{1}1^{1},8^{1}2^{1}1^{1},5^{1}4^{1}2^{1},7^{1}2^{2} and 42​314^{2}3^{1} in ℳi{\mathcal{M}}_{i} (and hence also in ℳ¯i\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{i}), so only when i=1i=1 does it have one of the possible orders 1,2,3,5,61,2,3,5,6 or 1111 of an element of LL. Conversely, it is easy to see that when LL is represented on the cosets of HH or H¯\overline{H} the generators xx and yy have cycle structures 33​123^{3}1^{2} and 24​132^{4}1^{3}, so LL is the monodromy group of at least one of the ten dessins, and this must be the pair ℳ1\mathcal{M}_{1} and ℳ¯1\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1}, with the two dessins corresponding to the two inequivalent representations of degree 1111.

Klein [51, §2] used a similar argument, based on a word equivalent to our y​z3yz^{3}, to show that the plane trees labelled II–VI in his diagram do not have monodromy group LL; he gave details only for tree V, corresponding to the dessin ℳ5{\mathcal{M}}_{5}. His paper is otherwise entirely devoted to the two trees labelled I (our Figure 1) with monodromy group LL, together with their minimal regular cover, which correspond to congruence subgroups of the modular group; the other eight trees, labelled II – VI and corresponding to noncongruence subgroups, are ignored, as are their monodromy groups.

In fact, the cycle structures of [x,y][x,y] given above show that for i=2,4,5i=2,4,5 and 66 the monodromy group GG is A11{\rm A}_{11}. Being transitive of prime degree, GG must be primitive; now a theorem of Jordan (see [72, Theorem 13.9], for example) shows that any finite primitive permutation group containing a cycle of prime length with at least three fixed points must contain the alternating group; in each of these four cases a suitable power of [x,y][x,y] has this property, so G≥A11G\geq{\rm A}_{11}. Since the generators xx and yy are even permutations, it follows that G=A11G={\rm A}_{11}. However, a separate argument is required for i=3i=3, for instance using the fact that in this case x​z3​x​z5xz^{3}xz^{5} has cycle structure 51​31​135^{1}3^{1}1^{3}. (The theorem of Jordan used here follows immediately from results in his papers [47, 48] published in 1871 and 1873, so Klein could have known and used this argument; for further historical comments on Jordan’s Theorem, and for a modern extension of it, see [41].)

The fact that these eight dessins have monodromy groups G≅A11G\cong{\rm A}_{11} shows that, as claimed above, they correspond to noncongruence subgroups of Γ\Gamma: the only nonabelian composition factors of any congruence quotient of Γ\Gamma are isomorphic to PSL2​(p){\rm PSL}_{2}(p) for primes p≥5p\geq 5 dividing the level [64], and by comparing orders it is easily seen that the simple group A11{\rm A}_{11} does not have this form.

4 Counting triples

We have already given a very simple argument showing why there are exactly ten dessins with the given characteristics. However, this simple example allows us an opportunity to illustrate another important enumeration technique based on character theory. Quite often, in more complicated cases where the degree or the genus is greater, this method is the only one available. It is based on Frobenius’s formula [25]

|𝒳|⋅|𝒴|⋅|𝒵||G|​∑χχ⁡(x)​χ​(y)​χ​(z)χ⁡(1)\displaystyle\frac{|{\mathcal{X}}|\cdot|{\mathcal{Y}}|\cdot|{\mathcal{Z}}|}{|G|}\sum_{\chi}\frac{\chi(x)\chi(y)\chi(z)}{\chi(1)} (2)

for the number of triples (x,y,z)∈𝒳×𝒴×𝒵(x,y,z)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{Z} with x​y​z=1xyz=1, where 𝒳\mathcal{X}, 𝒴\mathcal{Y} and 𝒵\mathcal{Z} are conjugacy classes in a finite group GG, and the sum is over the irreducible complex characters χ\chi of GG. (In specific applications, one often finds that many characters take the value 00 on 𝒳\mathcal{X}, 𝒴\mathcal{Y} or 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, so they can be omitted from the summation.) Since [25] was published 17 years after [51], this powerful technique was not available to Klein. Here we will show how it works in this fairly simple situation, ignoring results explained earlier; as a bonus we obtain the monodromy groups of all ten dessins.

Before doing this, we will give an alternative form of (2) which is sometimes more convenient, for instance when using the ATLAS [17] where orders of centralisers, rather than conjugacy classes, are given. We have |𝒳|=|G|/|C⁡(x)||\mathcal{X}|=|G|/|C(x)| where C​(x)=CG​(x)C(x)=C_{G}(x) denotes the centraliser of xx in GG, with similar equations for |𝒴||\mathcal{Y}| and |𝒵||\mathcal{Z}|, so we can rewrite  (2) as

|G|2|C⁡(x)|⋅|C⁡(y)|⋅|C⁡(z)|​∑χχ⁡(x)​χ​(y)​χ​(z)χ⁡(1).\displaystyle\frac{|G|^{2}}{|C(x)|\cdot|C(y)|\cdot|C(z)|}\sum_{\chi}\frac{\chi(x)\chi(y)\chi(z)}{\chi(1)}. (3)

If a dessin 𝒟\mathcal{D} has type (3,2,11)(3,2,11) and degree 1111, then its monodromy permutations x,y,z∈S11x,y,z\in{\rm S}_{11} satisfy the relations (1); having odd order, xx and zz are even, and hence so is yy, so the monodromy group G=⟨x,y,z⟩G=\langle x,y,z\rangle is a subgroup of A:=A11A:={\rm A}_{11}. Our aim is to count the triples xx, yy, zz in AA satisfying (1), and to determine the corresponding dessins 𝒟\mathcal{D} and their monodromy groups GG. In more general applications of (2) one has to exclude triples generating intransitive subgroups GG, since these cannot be monodromy groups of connected covers. However, here the fact that zz must be an 1111-cycle guarantees transitivity, so this problem does not arise. Since the orders 3,23,2 and 1111 of x,yx,y and zz are mutually coprime, GG must be perfect (have trivial abelianisation), and therefore cannot be solvable. If G≠AG\neq A then GG must be contained in a nonsolvable maximal subgroup MM of AA, of order divisible by 1111. According to the list of maximal subgroups of A11{\rm A}_{11} in [17], the only such maximal subgroups MM are isomorphic to the Mathieu group M11{\rm M}_{11}, forming two conjugacy classes of subgroups, of index 2520, transposed by Out​A{\rm Out}\,A. Similarly the list of maximal subgroups of M11{\rm M}_{11} in [17] tells us that if G≠MG\neq M then GG is isomorphic to L=PSL2​(11)L={\rm PSL}_{2}(11), each subgroup M≅M11M\cong{\rm M}_{11} containing one conjugacy class of such subgroups, of index 1212 in MM. Thus GG is equal to AA, or is isomorphic to M11{\rm M}_{11} or PSL2​(11){\rm PSL}_{2}(11); we will count the triples generating these three groups in turn, starting with the smallest.

Example 4.1

We will show that the group L=PSL2​(11)L={\rm PSL}_{2}(11) has, up to automorphisms (equivalently, up to conjugacy in PGL2​(11)≅Aut​L{\rm PGL}_{2}(11)\cong{\rm Aut}\,L), a single generating triple x,y,zx,y,z satisfying (1). The character table of LL, produced by GAP [28] and given here, has columns corresponding to the conjugacy classes, with the headings nna, nnb, etc. (nnA, nnB, etc in ATLAS notation [17]) indicating successive classes of elements of order nn; the rows, labelled X.j, correspond to irreducible characters χj\chi_{j} for j=1,2,…j=1,2,\ldots. The table includes entries A, ∗A :=(−1∓5)/2:=(-1\mp\sqrt{5})/2 and B,/B:=(−1±i11)/2{\rm B},/{\rm B}:=(-1\pm i\sqrt{11})/2, while a full stop denotes an entry 00.

       1a 3a 2a 5a 5b 6a 11a 11b

X.1     1  1  1  1  1  1   1   1
X.2     5 -1  1  .  .  1   B  /B
X.3     5 -1  1  .  .  1  /B   B
X.4    10  1 -2  .  .  1  -1  -1

X.6    11 -1 -1  1  1 -1   .   .
X.7    12  .  .  A *A  .   1   1
X.8    12  .  . *A  A  .   1   1

A = E(5)^2+E(5)^3
  = (-1-Sqrt(5))/2 = -1-b5
B = E(11)+E(11)^3+E(11)^4+E(11)^5+E(11)^9
  = (-1+Sqrt(-11))/2 = b11

In this example we take 𝒳\mathcal{X} and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} to be the classes 3a and 2a, and 𝒵\mathcal{Z} to be either of the classes 11a or 11b. For each choice of 𝒵\mathcal{Z} the character sum in formula (3) has the value

ΣL=1+(−1)⋅1⋅B5+(−1)⋅1⋅/B5+1⋅(−2)⋅(−1)10+1⋅2⋅(−1)10=1−B+/B5=65.\Sigma_{L}=1+\frac{(-1)\cdot 1\cdot{\rm B}}{5}+\frac{(-1)\cdot 1\cdot/{\rm B}}{5}+\frac{1\cdot(-2)\cdot(-1)}{10}+\frac{1\cdot 2\cdot(-1)}{10}=1-\frac{{\rm B}+/{\rm B}}{5}=\frac{6}{5}.

Now the centralisers CL​(x)C_{L}(x), CL​(y)C_{L}(y) and CL​(z)C_{L}(z) of typical elements x,yx,y and zz of 𝒳\mathcal{X}, 𝒴\mathcal{Y} and 𝒵\mathcal{Z} have orders 66, 1212 and 1111, so that

|L|2|C⁡(x)|⋅|C⁡(y)|⋅|C⁡(z)|=24⋅32⋅52⋅1126⋅12⋅11=2⋅52⋅11.\frac{|L|^{2}}{|C(x)|\cdot|C(y)|\cdot|C(z)|}=\frac{2^{4}\cdot 3^{2}\cdot 5^{2}\cdot 11^{2}}{6\cdot 12\cdot 11}=2\cdot 5^{2}\cdot 11.

Multiplying this by ΣL\Sigma_{L} gives 22⋅3⋅5⋅112^{2}\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 11 triples (x,y,z)∈𝒳×𝒴×𝒵(x,y,z)\in{\mathcal{X}}\times{\mathcal{Y}}\times{\mathcal{Z}} with x​y​z=1xyz=1 for each choice of 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, and hence 23⋅3⋅5⋅112^{3}\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 11 in total. Each triple must generate LL since this group has no proper subgroups of order divisible by 6666 (in fact, none of index less that 1111). Since Aut​L{\rm Aut}\,L acts semi-regularly on generating triples, dividing by its order |PGL2​(11)|=23⋅3⋅5⋅11|{\rm PGL}_{2}(11)|=2^{3}\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 11 shows that Aut​L{\rm Aut}\,L has a single orbit on such triples, as claimed.

Since the normal subgroups of any group Δ\Delta with quotient isomorphic to a group GG are in bijective correspondence with the orbits of Aut​G{\rm Aut}\,G, acting by composition, on epimorphisms Δ→G\Delta\to G, it follows that the triangle group

Δ:=Δ(3,2,11)=⟨X,Y,Z∣X3=Y2=Z11=XYZ=1⟩\Delta:=\Delta(3,2,11)=\langle X,Y,Z\mid X^{3}=Y^{2}=Z^{11}=XYZ=1\rangle

has a single normal subgroup with quotient isomorphic to LL. Now LL has two conjugacy classes of subgroups of index 1111, all isomorphic to A5{\rm A}_{5}, and these classes are transposed by its automorphism group PGL2​(11){\rm PGL}_{2}(11) (see [17] or [22, §259]); they lift to two conjugacy classes of subgroups of index 1111 in Δ\Delta, transposed by conjugation in the extended triangle group

Δ[3,2,11]=⟨R0,R1,R2∣Ri2=(R1R2)3=(R2R0)2=(R0R1)11=1⟩,\Delta[3,2,11]=\langle R_{0},R_{1},R_{2}\mid R_{i}^{2}=(R_{1}R_{2})^{3}=(R_{2}R_{0})^{2}=(R_{0}R_{1})^{11}=1\rangle,

which contains Δ\Delta with index 22, and they correspond to a chiral pair of dessins 𝒟\mathcal{D} of type (3,2,11)(3,2,11) degree 1111 with monodromy group isomorphic to LL. This calculation shows that they are the only such dessins, so they are the dessins ℳ1{\mathcal{M}}_{1} and ℳ¯1\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1} discussed earlier.

Example 4.3

Now we count triples satisfying (1) in A=A11A={\rm A}_{11}. In this case there are three conjugacy classes of elements of order 33, and two classes of elements of order 22. A simple argument shows that if elements x,y∈Ax,y\in A of orders 33 and 22 generate a transitive group than they must have cycle structures 33​123^{3}1^{2} and 24​132^{4}1^{3}, so they belong to the conjugacy classes 𝒳=3​c\mathcal{X}={\rm 3c} and 𝒴=2​b\mathcal{Y}={\rm 2b} of AA, while zz must be in one of the two classes 11a and 11b of 1111-cycles in AA.

The character table of AA is much too large to give here. However, the only irreducible characters χ\chi with χ⁡(x)​χ​(y)​χ​(z)≠0\chi(x)\chi(y)\chi(z)\neq 0 are the principal character χ1\chi_{1} and the characters χ2\chi_{2}, χ6\chi_{6} and χ11\chi_{11} of degrees 1010, 120120 and 210210, so we can give here the relevant portion of the character table, concerning these classes and characters:

ΣA:=∑χχ⁡(x)​χ​(y)​χ​(z)χ⁡(1)\Sigma_{A}:=\sum_{\chi}\frac{\chi(x)\chi(y)\chi(z)}{\chi(1)}

has the value

Multiplying this by 2​ΣA2\Sigma_{A} shows that the number of triples in AA satisfying (1) is

t:=29⋅34⋅53⋅7⋅11=10×11!.t:=2^{9}\cdot 3^{4}\cdot 5^{3}\cdot 7\cdot 11=10\times 11!.

From this total we must subtract the number of triples generating proper subgroups of AA. As we have seen, the only such subgroups are those isomorphic to PSL2​(11){\rm PSL}_{2}(11). Each subgroup L≅PSL2​(11)L\cong{\rm PSL}_{2}(11) in AA is contained in a unique subgroup M≅M11M\cong{\rm M}_{11}; there are two conjugacy classes of 2520 such subgroups MM in AA, each containing one conjugacy class of 1212 subgroups LL, so the number of such subgroups LL in AA is 2⋅2520⋅12=60480=26⋅33⋅5⋅72\cdot 2520\cdot 12=60480=2^{6}\cdot 3^{3}\cdot 5\cdot 7. As shown in Example 4.1, each subgroup LL is generated by 23⋅3⋅5⋅112^{3}\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 11 triples satisfying (1), so the number of triples in AA generating subgroups L≅PSL2​(11)L\cong{\rm PSL}_{2}(11) is 29⋅34⋅52⋅7⋅11=t/5=2×11!2^{9}\cdot 3^{4}\cdot 5^{2}\cdot 7\cdot 11=t/5=2\times 11!.

Since there are 10×11!10\times 11! triples in AA, of which 2×11!2\times 11! generate proper subgroups, there are 8×11!8\times 11! triples generating AA, forming eight orbits under Aut​A=S11{\rm Aut}\,A={\rm S}_{11}; these correspond to eight normal subgroups of Δ\Delta with quotient AA, and hence to eight regular dessins with (orientation-preserving) automorphism group AA. Now AA has a single conjugacy class of subgroups of index 1111, namely the natural point-stabilisers isomorphic to A10{\rm A}_{10}, so these lift to eight more conjugacy classes of subgroups of index 1111 in Δ\Delta, in addition to the two resulting from Example 4.1. These give eight more dessins 𝒟\mathcal{D} of type (3,2,11)(3,2,11) and degree 1111, all with monodromy group G≅A11G\cong{\rm A}_{11}. Thus we have a total of ten dessins of the required degree and type. This confirms the earlier enumeration, and also confirms that for ℳ1{\mathcal{M}}_{1} and ℳ¯1\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1} the monodromy group is PSL2​(11){\rm PSL}_{2}(11), whereas for the other eight dessins it is A11{\rm A}_{11}. Generating triples for these dessins are given in Subsection 14.1.

In each of the examples considered here, it was a fairly easy matter to evaluate the Frobenius formulae (2) or (3) by hand, but in other cases, if there are many non-zero summands, or if irrational character values arise, it may be necessary to appeal to GAP for this. For instance, the following GAP commands repeat the calculation in Example 4.1.


> G:=PSL(2,11);;
> T:=CharacterTable(G);;
> OrdersClassRepresentatives(T);
  [ 1, 3, 2, 5, 5, 6, 11, 11 ]
> ClassStructureCharTable(T,[2,3,7]);
  660
> ClassStructureCharTable(T,[2,3,8]);
  660

Here 2,3,72,3,7 and 2,3,82,3,8 indicate the positions of the chosen classes 𝒳\mathcal{X}, 𝒴\mathcal{Y} and 𝒵\mathcal{Z} in the preceding list. The double semicolons after a command ask GAP to execute the command but not to output the result. As in Example 4.1 we obtain 13201320 triples.

5 The dessins and their regular covers

Our enumeration of triples in LL shows that there is a single regular dessin ℛ1\mathcal{R}_{1} of type (3,2,11)(3,2,11) with automorphism group L≅PSL2​(11)L\cong{\rm PSL}_{2}(11); this is the minimal regular cover of each of the two dessins ℳ1\mathcal{M}_{1} and ℳ¯1\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1} with monodromy group LL, and these are quotients of ℛ1\mathcal{R}_{1} by non-conjugate subgroups of LL isomorphic to A5{\rm A}_{5}. By the Riemann–Hurwitz formula a regular dessin of this type with automorphism group GG has genus 1+5132​|G|1+\frac{5}{132}|G|, in this case equal to 2626. By its uniqueness, or by an observation of Singerman [70] concerning triples in PSL2​(q){\rm PSL}_{2}(q), ℛ1\mathcal{R}_{1} is regular as a map, corresponding to a subgroup of Δ\Delta which is normal in the extended triangle group Δ⁡[3,2,11]\Delta[3,2,11]. It is, in fact, the dual of the unique orientable regular map of genus 2626 and type {3,11}\{3,11\}, denoted by R26.2 in Conder’s catalogue of regular maps [16]; its full automorphism group as a map, containing also the automorphisms reversing the orientation, is isomorphic to PGL2​(11){\rm PGL}_{2}(11). For a drawing of R26.2 (combinatorially though not geometrically correct), with 6060 1111-valent vertices, 330330 edges and 220220 triangular faces, see [40, Fig. 6 and Table 1], where it is shown as a 198198-gon with side identifications; in this paper, Ivrissimtzis, Singerman and Strudwick reinterpret the regular maps associated with Klein’s papers [50] and [51] in terms of Farey fractions.

The eight dessins 𝒟\mathcal{D} with monodromy group A11{\rm A}_{11} consist of the three chiral pairs ℳi\mathcal{M}_{i} and ℳ¯i\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{i} with i=2,3,4i=2,3,4, together with ℳ5\mathcal{M}_{5} and ℳ6\mathcal{M}_{6}. The minimal regular covers of these dessins are eight regular dessins ℛ\mathcal{R} of genus 756 001756\,001, and each dessin 𝒟\mathcal{D} is the quotient of ℛ\mathcal{R} by a subgroup isomorphic to A10{\rm A}_{10} in its automorphism group A11{\rm A}_{11}. These eight dessins ℛ\mathcal{R} are mutually non-isomorphic, since A11{\rm A}_{11} has a unique conjugacy class of such subgroups (the point-stabilisers in the natural representation), so that any isomorphism between the dessins ℛ\mathcal{R} would induce an isomorphism between their quotients 𝒟\mathcal{D}, which is visibly impossible (see Figure 3).

The bilateral symmetry of the dessins ℳ5\mathcal{M}_{5} and ℳ6\mathcal{M}_{6} is easily explained: in each case there is a permutation in S11S_{11} simultaneously inverting the generating permutations xx and yy for the monodromy group A11A_{11}, and this induces an isomorphism of the dessin with its mirror image. (Of course, since y2=1y^{2}=1, inverting yy means the same as commuting with it.) Equivalently, each of the corresponding map subgroups MM in Δ⁡(3,2,11)\Delta(3,2,11) is contained with index 22 in a subgroup of Δ⁡[3,2,11]\Delta[3,2,11] which induces this isomorphism. The same applies to the regular covers of ℳ5\mathcal{M}_{5} and ℳ6\mathcal{M}_{6}, each corresponding to the core (intersection of conjugates) of MM in Δ⁡(3,2,11)\Delta(3,2,11); the other six regular covers form three chiral pairs, like their quotients.

For example, Figure 7 shows the map ℳ5\mathcal{M}_{5} corresponding to 𝒟5\mathcal{D}_{5}; directed edges are labelled 1,2,…,111,2,\ldots,11, so that

x=(1,11,6)​(2,5,4)​(7,10,8)andy=(1,5)​(2,3)​(6,10)​(8,9),x=(1,11,6)(2,5,4)(7,10,8)\quad{\rm and}\quad y=(1,5)(2,3)(6,10)(8,9),

and hence

z=(1,2,…,11).z=(1,2,\ldots,11).

The permutation t=(1,6)​(2,8)​(3,9)​(4,7)​(5,10)t=(1,6)(2,8)(3,9)(4,7)(5,10) inverts xx and yy, inducing the automorphism of ℳ5\mathcal{M}_{5} given by reflection in the vertical axis. The situation is similar for ℳ6\mathcal{M}_{6}, with generators

6 Computations and Galois orbits

Each of the ten dessins 𝒟\mathcal{D} discussed here represents a Belyĭ function, in this case an 1111-sheeted covering β:Σ→Σ\beta:\Sigma\to\Sigma. As such, β\beta is a rational function of degree 1111, and having a single pole at ∞\infty it must be a polynomial, called a Shabat polynomial.

A computation using MAPLE shows that the Shabat polynomial P:Σ→ΣP:\Sigma\to\Sigma for the dessins ℳ1\mathcal{M}_{1} and ℳ¯1\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1} in Figure 2 has the form

P=1212​314​p13​p23​p3P=\frac{1}{2^{12}3^{14}}p_{1}^{3}p_{2}^{3}p_{3}

where

p1​(x)=2​x+(11−3​−11),p_{1}(x)=2x+(11-3\sqrt{-11}),
p2​(x)=2​x2−(11−3​−11)​x−(22+6​−11),p_{2}(x)=2x^{2}-(11-3\sqrt{-11})x-(22+6\sqrt{-11}),
p3​(x)=x2+11​x+(55+9​−11),p_{3}(x)=x^{2}+11x+(55+9\sqrt{-11}),

so that

P−1=−1211​314​q12​q22​q3P-1=-\frac{1}{2^{11}3^{14}}q_{1}^{2}q_{2}^{2}q_{3}

where

q1​(x)=2​x+(5+3​−11),q_{1}(x)=2x+(5+3\sqrt{-11}),
q2​(x)=2​x3+(15−3​−11)​x2−(12−12​−11)​x+(56+96​−11),q_{2}(x)=2x^{3}+(15-3\sqrt{-11})x^{2}-(12-12\sqrt{-11})x+(56+96\sqrt{-11}),
OPENq3​(x)=2​x3−18​x2+(21+45​−11)​x−(175+279)​−11).q_{3}(x)=2x^{3}-18x^{2}+(21+45\sqrt{-11})x-(175+279)\sqrt{-11}).

The two possible choices for −11\sqrt{-11} give the two dessins. They are defined over ℚ⁡(−11){\mathbb{Q}}(\sqrt{-11}) (which is not surprising, since −11\sqrt{-11} appears in the character table of PSL2​(11){\rm PSL}_{2}(11)), and they are transposed by the Galois group of this field, generated by complex conjugation.

In each dessin, the black vertices are at the zeros of PP: the three vertices of valency 33 correspond to the zeros of p1p_{1} and p2p_{2}, each appearing with multiplicity 33 as a zero of PP, and the two vertices of valency 11 are at the zeros of p3p_{3}. The white vertices are at the zeros of P−1P-1: the four vertices of valency 22 correspond to the zeros of q1q_{1} and q2q_{2}, each appearing with multiplicity 22 as a zero of P−1P-1, and the three vertices of valency 11 are the zeros of q3q_{3}. The unique face-centre is at ∞\infty, the pole of PP with multiplicity 1111. For example, Figure 8 shows such a geometrically correct version of ℳ1\mathcal{M}_{1} in the plane ℂ\mathbb{C}. With a few exceptions (Figures 15, 16 and 18) all plane trees, dessins and maps shown in this paper are only combinatorially and topologically correct.

The other eight dessins form a single Galois orbit. A computation using Pari/GP produced several defining polynomials for the field of moduli corresponding to this orbit, of which the simplest appears to be

Z8+2​Z6−3​Z5+10​Z4−14​Z3+14​Z2−8​Z+1.Z^{8}+2Z^{6}-3Z^{5}+10Z^{4}-14Z^{3}+14Z^{2}-8Z+1.

The Galois group of this field is S8{\rm S}_{8}, inducing all possible permutations of the eight dessins. The field does not contain ℚ⁡(−11){\mathbb{Q}}(\sqrt{-11}), nor, indeed, does it contain ℚ⁡(21){\mathbb{Q}}(\sqrt{21}), even though 21\sqrt{21} appears in the character table of A11{\rm A}_{11}.

7 Other related dessins of degree 1111

The ten dessins discussed in this paper are not the only dessins of degree 1111 and type (3,2,r)(3,2,r) for some rr, the least common multiple of the face valencies. It is easy to see that in any such dessin the distribution of valencies of the black vertices must be 33​123^{3}1^{2}, while that of the white vertices must be 24​132^{4}1^{3} or 25​112^{5}1^{1}. In the former case we obtain the ten dessins based on Klein’s diagram, all with r=11r=11, but in the latter case we have planar dessins with two faces, rather than one, not considered by Klein.

The maps corresponding to these additional dessins can all be formed from the basic map ℳ0{\mathcal{M}}_{0} in Figure 4 by adding vertices of valency 11 to two of its free edges, as in the construction of the maps ℳ=ℳi{\mathcal{M}}={\mathcal{M}}_{i} and ℳ¯i\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{i}, and then joining together two of the remaining three free edges to form a single non-free edge. Equivalently one can perform the latter operation, in three possible ways, on each of the ten maps ℳ{\mathcal{M}}, giving 3030 maps of the required form. However, one finds that some of these maps are mutually isomorphic, and that up to isomorphism we obtain just 1616 dessins (confirmed using GAP), consisting of four with bilateral symmetry (in the first row of Figure 9) and six chiral pairs (those in the second row and their mirror images).

There are six where the face valency split is 10+110+1, three each where it is 9+29+2 or 7+47+4, and two each where it is 8+38+3 or 6+56+5. These dessins correspond to sixteen more conjugacy classes of subgroups of index 1111 in the modular group Γ\Gamma, in addition to the ten corresponding to Klein’s plane trees. (This is confirmed by [31, Theorem 1], which gives a recurrence relation for the number NnN_{n} of subgroups of index nn in Γ\Gamma; here N11=286N_{11}=286, corresponding to 10+16=2610+16=26 conjugacy classes each containing 1111 subgroups.) In all cases except 10+110+1, one of the face valencies is a prime pp, and z11−pz^{11-p} is a pp-cycle with 11−p≥311-p\geq 3 fixed points; being transitive of prime degree the monodromy group G=⟨x,y⟩G=\langle x,y\rangle is primitive, so it follows from Jordan’s Theorem and the fact that yy is odd that G=S11G={\rm S}_{11}; in the case 10+110+1 we may apply an extension of Jordan’s Theorem in [41] to the cycles of length 1010 and 1111 to show that GG acts as S11{\rm S}_{11} or AGL1​(11){\rm AGL}_{1}(11), with the latter excluded since it has no elements of order 33. It follows that these dessins correspond to non-congruence subgroups of Γ\Gamma. Their regular covers have genus

1+(r−6)12​r​11!1+\frac{(r-6)}{12r}11!
