8 Monodromy groups of dessins of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) and degree pp

We can generalise our earlier arguments by considering dessins 𝒟\mathcal{D} of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) and degree pp for all primes pp, not just for p=11p=11. The monodromy group GG of such a dessin 𝒟\mathcal{D} must be a transitive permutation group of degree pp, and must be perfect if p>3p>3, as we will assume, since 3,23,2 and pp are mutually coprime. The transitive groups of prime degree pp are all known (modulo a very difficult number-theoretic problem which we will discuss in the next section), and are described in [13, 23, 39], for example. They are as follows:

Theorem 8.1

The transitive permutation groups GG of prime degree are the following:

  • (a)

    subgroups GG of AGL1​(p){\rm AGL}_{1}(p) containing the translation subgroup;

  • (b)

    G=ApG={\rm A}_{p} or Sp{\rm S}_{p} for a prime p≥5p\geq 5;

  • (c)

    G=PSL2​(11)G={\rm PSL}_{2}(11), M11{\rm M}_{11} or M23{\rm M}_{23} with p=11,11p=11,11 or 2323;

  • (d)

    groups GG such that PSLn​(q)≤G≤P​Γ​Ln​(q){\rm PSL}_{n}(q)\leq G\leq{\rm P\Gamma L}_{n}(q) where the degree (qn−1)/(q−1)(q^{n}-1)/(q-1) of its natural representation(s) is prime.

By a result of Galois [26], the solvable groups of prime degree pp are those in (a). Burnside (see [11] or [12, §251]) showed that any nonsolvable group GG of prime degree pp is doubly transitive; in this case a straightforward argument shows that S≤G≤Aut​SS\leq G\leq{\rm Aut}\,S where SS, the unique minimal normal subgroup of GG, is a doubly transitive nonabelian simple group. By the classification of finite simple groups, the possibilities for SS are S=ApS={\rm A}_{p} for a prime p≥5p\geq 5, giving the groups in (b), the three groups S=GS=G in (c), and S=PSLn​(q)S={\rm PSL}_{n}(q), giving the groups in (d).

In (a) and (b) these are the natural actions of the groups listed. In (c), PSL2​(11){\rm PSL}_{2}(11) has two actions of degree 1111, on the cosets of two conjugacy classes of subgroups isomorphic to A5{\rm A}_{5}, while the Mathieu groups M11{\rm M}_{11} and M23{\rm M}_{23} act on Steiner systems with 1111 and 2323 points. In (d) the groups act on the points of the projective geometry ℙn−1​(𝔽q){\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}({\mathbb{F}}_{q}), with a second dual action on its hyperplanes if n≥3n\geq 3. In particular, since Out​S{\rm Out}\,S is solvable in all cases, we have:

Corollary 8.2

The only perfect groups of prime degree are the simple groups Ap{\rm A}_{p}, PSL2​(11){\rm PSL}_{2}(11), M11{\rm M}_{11}, M23{\rm M}_{23} and PSLn​(q){\rm PSL}_{n}(q) appearing in parts (b), (c) and (d) of Theorem 8.1.

These simple groups GG all have elements xx, yy and zz of orders 33, 22 and pp since they have orders divisible by these primes, so there remain the questions of whether there exist such triples with x​y​z=1xyz=1, whether these can generate GG, and if so, of determining (or at least enumerating) the corresponding dessins 𝒟\mathcal{D}. We will address these questions, on a case by case basis, later in this and the following two sections. First we calculate the genera of these maps and of their regular covers.

If xx and yy have cycle structures 3a​1α3^{a}1^{\alpha} and 2b​1β2^{b}1^{\beta}, with α=p−3​a\alpha=p-3a and β=p−2​b\beta=p-2b, then 𝒟\mathcal{D} has p−2​ap-2a black vertices, p−bp-b white vertices, pp edges and one face, so it has Euler characteristic

χ=(p−2​a)+(p−b)−p+1=p−2​a−b+1=4​α+3​β−p6+1\chi=(p-2a)+(p-b)-p+1=p-2a-b+1\,=\frac{4\alpha+3\beta-p}{6}+1

and hence genus

1−χ2=2​a+b+1−p2=p−4​α−3​β+612.1-\frac{\chi}{2}=\frac{2a+b+1-p}{2}\;=\frac{p-4\alpha-3\beta+6}{12}.

(Note that this implies that 2​a+b≥p−12a+b\geq p-1, or equivalently 4​α+3​β≤p+64\alpha+3\beta\leq p+6.) If it exists, such a dessin 𝒟\mathcal{D} has a regular cover ℛ\mathcal{R} of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) with automorphism group GG. Since ℛ\mathcal{R} has |G|/3|G|/3 black vertices of degree 3, |G|/2|G|/2 white vertices of degree 2, |G||G| edges, and |G|/p|G|/p faces of degree pp, its Euler characteristic is

χ=(13+12+1p−1)⋅|G|=6−p6​p​|G|,\chi=\left(\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{p}-1\right)\cdot|G|=\frac{6-p}{6p}|G|,

so that its genus is

g=1−χ2=p−612​p​|G|+1.g=1-\frac{\chi}{2}=\frac{p-6}{12p}|G|+1.

8.1 Case (c): sporadic examples

It is convenient to deal with case (c) first. We have seen in Examples 4.1 and 4.2, that if p=11p=11 then M11{\rm M}_{11} does not arise as the monodromy group of a dessin of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) and degree p=11p=11, whereas PSL2​(11){\rm PSL}_{2}(11) does, for the chiral pair ℳ1{\mathcal{M}}_{1} and ℳ¯1\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1}. The Frobenius formula (2) eliminates M23{\rm M}_{23}: this group contains no triples (x,y,z)(x,y,z) of type (3,2,23)(3,2,23) such that x​y​z=1xyz=1.

8.2 Case (b): alternating groups

In case (b) we have G=ApG={\rm A}_{p} for some prime pp. The following result shows that almost all such groups arise as monodromy groups in the required context.

Theorem 8.3

For each prime p≠2,3,7p\neq 2,3,7 there is a dessin 𝒟\mathcal{D} of degree pp and type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) with monodromy group Ap{\rm A}_{p}.

Proof. First suppose that p≡2p\equiv 2 mod (3)(3), say p=3​k+2p=3k+2. There is an obvious map for p=5p=5, so we may assume that p≥11p\geq 11, and hence k≥3k\geq 3. Let 𝒟\mathcal{D} be the map on the left in Figure 10, where there are kk vertices of degree 33, so that 𝒟\mathcal{D} has passport (3k​12,2k+1​1k,p1)(3^{k}1^{2},2^{k+1}1^{k},p^{1}). We aim to show that its monodromy group GG is Ap{\rm A}_{p}. By Corollary 8.2 and the discussion of sporadic examples in case (c) it is sufficient to show that GG is not PSL2​(11){\rm PSL}_{2}(11) acting with degree 1111 or a group PSLn​(q){\rm PSL}_{n}(q) acting naturally for some n≥2n\geq 2 and prime power qq. In fact, when p=11p=11, so that k=3k=3, 𝒟\mathcal{D} is isomorphic to ℳ¯3\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{3} in Figure 3, and we have seen that this has monodromy group A11{\rm A}_{11}. We may therefore suppose, for a contradiction, that G=PSLn​(q)G={\rm PSL}_{n}(q) acting naturally, and that p≥17p\geq 17, so that k≥5k\geq 5.

If π\pi denotes the permutation character of Sp{\rm S}_{p}, counting fixed points of elements, we see that the involution yy corresponding to 𝒟\mathcal{D} has fixed point ratio

π⁡(y)π⁡(1)=kp=k3​k+2≥517.\frac{\pi(y)}{\pi(1)}=\frac{k}{p}=\frac{k}{3k+2}\geq\frac{5}{17}.

We will compare this with the corresponding values for involutions in PSLn​(q){\rm PSL}_{n}(q). Any involution in PSL2​(q){\rm PSL}_{2}(q) fixes at most two points, so n≠2n\neq 2 since π⁡(y)=k≥5\pi(y)=k\geq 5. For n≥3n\geq 3 the involutions g∈PSLn​(q)g\in{\rm PSL}_{n}(q) have fixed point ratios π⁡(g)/π⁡(1)\pi(g)/\pi(1) bounded above by

be=qn−2+qn−3+⋯+q+1qn−1+qn−2+⋯+q+1orbo=(qn−3+⋯+q+1)+(q+1)qn−1+qn−2+⋯+q+1b_{e}=\frac{q^{n-2}+q^{n-3}+\cdots+q+1}{q^{n-1}+q^{n-2}+\cdots+q+1}\quad\hbox{or}\quad b_{o}=\frac{(q^{n-3}+\cdots+q+1)+(q+1)}{q^{n-1}+q^{n-2}+\cdots+q+1}

as qq is even or odd: these bounds are attained when gg fixes a hyperplane or two disjoint subspaces of dimensions n−3n-3 and 11, respectively, corresponding to matrices in SLn​(q){\rm SL}_{n}(q) with Jordan normal form given by block matrices

(JOOI)whereJ=(1101)or(−100−1)andI=In−2.\Big(\,\begin{array}[]{cc}J&O\\ O&I\end{array}\,\Big)\quad\hbox{where}\quad J=\Big(\,\begin{array}[]{cc}1&1\\ 0&1\end{array}\,\Big)\quad\hbox{or}\quad\Big(\,\begin{array}[]{cc}-1&0\\ 0&-1\end{array}\,\Big)\quad\hbox{and}\quad I=I_{n-2}.

It is straightforward to check that if qq is odd then bo<5/17b_{o}<5/17 and hence G≠PSLn​(q)G\neq{\rm PSL}_{n}(q), unless n=q=3n=q=3, when bo=5/13b_{o}=5/13; however, this exceptional case corresponds to p=13≢2p=13\not\equiv 2 mod (3)(3). Thus qq is even, so q=2q=2 since be<1/qb_{e}<1/q. This gives 3​k+2=p=2n−13k+2=p=2^{n}-1 and hence 2n≡02^{n}\equiv 0 mod (3)(3), which is impossible.

We can apply a similar argument when p≡1p\equiv 1 mod (3)(3), say p=3​k+1p=3k+1. We may assume that p≥13p\geq 13, that is, k≥4k\geq 4. By deleting a vertex of valency 11 from 𝒟\mathcal{D} we obtain the map 𝒟′{\mathcal{D}}^{\prime} of degree pp, type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) and passport (3k​11,2k​1k+1,p1)(3^{k}1^{1},2^{k}1^{k+1},p^{1}) shown on the right in Figure 10. The corresponding involution yy now has fixed point ratio

π⁡(y)π⁡(1)=k+1p=k+13​k+1≥513.\frac{\pi(y)}{\pi(1)}=\frac{k+1}{p}=\frac{k+1}{3k+1}\geq\frac{5}{13}.

As before, if G=PSLn​(q)G={\rm PSL}_{n}(q) then π⁡(y)>2\pi(y)>2 implies that n≥3n\geq 3. We have already seen that if qq is odd then bo<5/17b_{o}<5/17, so that bo<5/13b_{o}<5/13 and hence G≠PSLn​(q)G\neq{\rm PSL}_{n}(q), unless n=q=3n=q=3; however, in this case p=13p=13, and GAP shows that 𝒟′{\mathcal{D}}^{\prime} has monodromy group A13{\rm A}_{13} rather than PSL3​(3){\rm PSL}_{3}(3), so qq must be even. Again, q=2q=2 since be<1/qb_{e}<1/q, so if any element of G=PSLn​(2)G={\rm PSL}_{n}(2) has fixed points they must form a projective subspace. Thus k=π⁡(y)k=\pi(y) is odd and hence p=3​k+1p=3k+1 is even, a contradiction. □\square

It is easy to see that there is no corresponding dessin if p=2p=2 or 33. When p=7p=7 there is a chiral pair of dessins of the required degree and type, represented by 𝒟′{\mathcal{D}}^{\prime} in Figure 10 with k=2k=2, but they have monodromy group PSL2​(7){\rm PSL}_{2}(7), not A7{\rm A}_{7} (which is not a Hurwitz group). Simple modifications to the dessins in Figure 10 show that in the proof of Theorem 8.3 the number of choices for 𝒟\mathcal{D} and 𝒟′\mathcal{D}^{\prime} increases exponentially with pp, even though that construction produces only planar dessins.

8.3 Case (d): projective groups

For the rest of this section, we will therefore assume that we are in case (d), with G=PSLn​(q)G={\rm PSL}_{n}(q) acting on points or hyperplanes of ℙn−1​(𝔽q){\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}({\mathbb{F}}_{q}). (This case, together with associated number theoretic estimates and computer searches covered in Section 9, is investigated in more detail in [46].)

Warning: here, in spite of an almost universal convention on notation, the unnamed prime of which qq is a power is not the prime pp; instead, pp will denote the degree (qn−1)/(q−1)(q^{n}-1)/(q-1) of GG.

Before proceeding, we need to make a short digression into number theory. Let us define a prime pp to be projective if it has the form

p=qn−1q−1=1+q+q2+⋯+qn−1p=\frac{q^{n}-1}{q-1}=1+q+q^{2}+\cdots+q^{n-1}

for some prime power q≥2q\geq 2 and integer n≥2n\geq 2. These primes include the Fermat primes p=22k+1p=2^{2^{k}}+1 with q=22kq=2^{2^{k}} and n=2n=2, the Mersenne primes p=2n−1p=2^{n}-1 with q=2q=2 and nn prime, together with other examples with q,n≥3q,n\geq 3, such as p=13p=13 with q=n=3q=n=3, and p=31p=31 with q=5q=5 and n=3n=3 (notice that p=31p=31 is also a Mersenne prime). Of course, it is an open problem whether there are infinitely many Fermat or Mersenne primes; at the time of writing, only five Fermat primes (with k=0,…,4k=0,\ldots,4) and 5151 Mersenne primes are known to exist. More generally, the existence of infinitely many projective primes seems to be an open problem. In [46] we give heuristic arguments based on the Bateman–Horn Conjecture, together with associated computational evidence, to support a conjecture that there are infinitely many such primes, even for each fixed prime n≥3n\geq 3. These are summarised in the next section. However, first we need to prove some necessary conditions for (qn−1)/(q−1)(q^{n}-1)/(q-1) to be prime.

Lemma 8.4

Given integers n≥2n\geq 2 and e≥1e\geq 1, the polynomial

f⁡(t)=tn​e−1te−1=1+te+t2​e+⋯+t(n−1)​ef(t)=\frac{t^{ne}-1}{t^{e}-1}=1+t^{e}+t^{2e}+\cdots+t^{(n-1)e}

is irreducible in ℤ⁡[t]{\mathbb{Z}}[t] if and only if nn is prime and ee is a power ni​(i≥0)n^{i}\;(i\geq 0) of nn.

Proof. If k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} the cyclotomic polynomial Φk​(x)\Phi_{k}(x) is, by definition, the polynomial with integer coefficients whose roots are the primitive kkth roots of unity. It is irreducible and has degree φ⁡(k)\varphi(k), where φ\varphi is the Euler totient function. For any n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} we have xn−1=∏d|nΦd​(x)x^{n}-1=\prod_{d|n}\Phi_{d}(x) (see [8, §5.2.1] or [66, §4.3, Problem 26]). Putting x=tex=t^{e} gives

f⁡(t)=tn​e−1te−1=∏dΦd​(t),f(t)=\frac{t^{ne}-1}{t^{e}-1}=\prod_{d}\Phi_{d}(t), (4)

with the product over all dd which divide n​ene but not ee. Thus ff is irreducible if and only if there is just one such divisor dd (which is n​ene itself, of course). By considering the prime power decompositions of ee and n​ene one can see that this happens if and only if nn is prime and ee is a power of nn. □\square

Lemma 8.5

Let q=req=r^{e} where rr is prime, and let n≥2n\geq 2. If p=(qn−1)/(q−1)p=(q^{n}-1)/(q-1) is prime then

  • (a)

    nn is prime and ee is a power ni​(i≥0)n^{i}\;(i\geq 0) of nn;

  • (b)

    q≢1q\not\equiv 1 mod (n)(n);

  • (c)

    PSLn​(q)=SLn​(q){\rm PSL}_{n}(q)={\rm SL}_{n}(q).

Proof. (a) This follows from Lemma 8.4, using the fact that p=f⁡(r)=∏dΦd​(r)p=f(r)=\prod_{d}\Phi_{d}(r) as in (4), with each Φd​(r)≠±1\Phi_{d}(r)\neq\pm 1. (To see the latter, note that Φd​(r)=∏ζ(r−ζ)\Phi_{d}(r)=\prod_{\zeta}(r-\zeta) where ζ\zeta ranges over the primitive dd-th roots of unity, so that |r−ζ|>1|r-\zeta|>1 for each ζ\zeta.)

(b) If q≡1q\equiv 1 mod (n)(n) then p=1+q+⋯+qn−1≡0p=1+q+\cdots+q^{n-1}\equiv 0 mod (n)(n) with p>np>n.

(c) For any qq and nn we have PSLn​(q)=SLn​(q)/Z{\rm PSL}_{n}(q)={\rm SL}_{n}(q)/Z, where Z={λ​I∈GLn​(q)∣λn=1}≅CdZ=\{\lambda I\in{\rm GL}_{n}(q)\mid\lambda^{n}=1\}\cong{\rm C}_{d} is the centre of SLn​(q){\rm SL}_{n}(q) and d=gcd⁡(q−1,n)d=\gcd(q-1,n). If pp is prime then d=1d=1 by (a) and (b). □\square

9 The Bateman–Horn Conjecture

The Bateman–Horn Conjecture [3] is a quantified version of Schinzel’s Hypothesis H [68]. Both of them concern the question of whether a finite set of polynomials f1​(t),…,fk​(t)∈ℤ⁡[t]f_{1}(t),\ldots,f_{k}(t)\in{\mathbb{Z}}[t] simultaneously take prime values fi​(t)f_{i}(t) at infinitely many t∈ℕt\in{\mathbb{N}}. (Schinzels’s Hypothesis H is in turn a generalisation of the Bunyakovsky Conjecture (1857, see [9, 10]), which deals with the case k=1k=1.) Clearly the following conditions are necessary for this to happen:

  • •

    the leading coefficient of each fif_{i} is positive,

  • •

    each fif_{i} is irreducible,

  • •

    f:=f1​…​fkf:=f_{1}\ldots f_{k} is not identically zero modulo any prime.

In any specific case, the final condition can be verified as follows: ff cannot be identically zero modulo any prime p>deg⁡(f)p>\deg(f) unless pp divides all of its coefficients, and for the remaining primes pp one can simply evaluate f⁡(t)f(t) at each element t∈ℤpt\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{p}. Schinzel (following Bunyakovsky in the case k=1k=1) conjectured that these conditions are also sufficient. If true, this would imply several other conjectures in Number Theory. For instance, taking f1​(t)=t2+1f_{1}(t)=t^{2}+1 would imply the Euler–Landau Conjecture that there are infinitely many primes of the form t2+1t^{2}+1, while taking f1​(t)=tf_{1}(t)=t and f2​(t)=t+2f_{2}(t)=t+2 or 2​t+12t+1 would imply the conjectures that there are infinitely many twin primes and Sophie Germain primes.

The Bateman–Horn Conjecture goes further by proposing a heuristic estimate, based on the Prime Number Theorem, for the number Q⁡(x)Q(x) of t≤xt\leq x in ℕ\mathbb{N} such that each fi​(t)f_{i}(t) is prime. This has the form

Q⁡(x)∼E⁡(x):=C∏i=1kdeg⁡fi​∫2xd​t(ln⁡t)kasx→∞Q(x)\sim E(x):=\frac{C}{\prod_{i=1}^{k}\deg f_{i}}\int_{2}^{x}\frac{dt}{(\ln t)^{k}}\quad\hbox{as}\quad x\to\infty (5)

where

C=C⁡(f1,…,fk):=∏r(1−1r)−k​(1−ωf​(r)r)C=C(f_{1},\ldots,f_{k}):=\prod_{r}\left(1-\frac{1}{r}\right)^{-k}\left(1-\frac{\omega_{f}(r)}{r}\right) (6)

with the product over all primes rr, and ωf​(r)\omega_{f}(r) is the number of t∈𝔽rt\in{\mathbb{F}}_{r} such that f⁡(t)=0f(t)=0. If the above conditions on f1,…,fkf_{1},\ldots,f_{k} are satisfied then the infinite product in (6) converges to a limit C>0C>0 (this is far from obvious: see [2], Theorem 5.4.3); since the integral in (5) diverges as x→∞x\to\infty, this would imply that f1​(t),…,fk​(t)f_{1}(t),\ldots,f_{k}(t) are simultaneously prime for infinitely many t∈ℕt\in{\mathbb{N}}. So far, these three conjectures have been proved only in the case k=1k=1, deg⁡f1=1\deg f_{1}=1: in the case of the Bunyakovsky and Schinzel conjectures, this is Dirichlet’s theorem on primes in an arithmetic progression a​t+bat+b; in the case of Bateman–Horn it is equivalent to the stronger form of this theorem, giving an asymptotically equal distribution of primes among the congruence classes of units bb mod (a)(a) (see [8, §5.3.2] for a proof, and [71] for an error estimate).

Nevertheless, the Bateman–Horn Conjecture has provided estimates remarkably close to experimental evidence in cases such as the twin primes conjecture. To give just one example, the number of twin prime pairs up to 101810^{18} is 808 675 888 577 436808\,675\,888\,577\,436 (entry A007508 of [67]), while the Bateman–Horn estimate gives 808 675 900 456 220808\,675\,900\,456\,220. The relative error is −0.000000147%-0.000000147\%. See also [2, Figure 10]. The constant CC is, in this case, equal to 1.320323630​…1.320323630\ldots, while C/2=0.660161815​…C/2=0.660161815\ldots is traditionally called the “twin primes constant”.

Remark 9.1

Li [57] has suggested a modified version of the Bateman–Horn Conjecture in which ∏ideg⁡fi\prod_{i}\deg f_{i} in the denominator is removed and each factor 1/ln⁡(t)1/\ln(t) within the integral is replaced with 1/ln⁡(fi​(t))1/\ln(f_{i}(t)); the lower limit of integration may also be adjusted to avoid a logarithmic singularity at fi​(t)=1f_{i}(t)=1. The result is asymptotically equivalent to the original conjecture, but in cases such as Sophie Germain primes, involving a non-monic polynomial fif_{i}, the approximation is significantly better.

In our case, if we take k=2k=2, with f1​(t)=tf_{1}(t)=t and f2​(t)=1+te+t2​e+⋯+t(n−1)​ef_{2}(t)=1+t^{e}+t^{2e}+\cdots+t^{(n-1)e} for a fixed prime n≥3n\geq 3 and a fixed exponent e=nie=n^{i}, then f2f_{2} is irreducible by Lemma 8.4, so the conjecture gives an estimate E⁡(x)E(x) for the number Q⁡(x)Q(x) of primes t≤xt\leq x such that 1+q+q2+⋯+qn−11+q+q^{2}+\cdots+q^{n-1} is prime, where q=teq=t^{e}. Computer searches confirm the obvious guess that Q⁡(x)Q(x) grows fastest when ee and nn take their minimum values n=3n=3 and e=1e=1 (so qq is prime), so that f2​(t)=1+t+t2f_{2}(t)=1+t+t^{2}. For example,44 4 The computation was carried out by our colleague Jean Bétréma [5]. He used the system Julia which, on this occasion, turned out to be more efficient than Maple. all except 301301 of the 1 974 3111\,974\,311 projective primes p≤1018p\leq 10^{18} have the form p=1+q+q2p=1+q+q^{2} for some prime qq.

Putting n=3n=3 and e=1e=1, so that f=t⁡(1+t+t2)f=t(1+t+t^{2}), we get

ωf​(r)={3if ​r≡1​ mod ​(3),2for ​r=3,1otherwise.\omega_{f}(r)\,=\,\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}3&\mbox{if }r\equiv 1\mbox{ mod }(3),\\ 2&\mbox{for }r=3,\\ 1&\mbox{otherwise}.\end{array}\right.

We use Maple to calculate C≈1.52173006C\approx 1.52173006 (taking the product over all primes r<109r<10^{9}) and ∫2x(ln⁡t)−2​𝑑t\int_{2}^{x}(\ln t)^{-2}dt (by numerical quadrature) for x=i⋅1010​(i=1,2,…,10)x=i\cdot 10^{10}\;(i=1,2,\ldots,10). In Table 2 the resulting estimates E⁡(x)E(x) are compared with the true values Q⁡(x)Q(x) found by computer searches. (Here, Li’s improvement in Remark 9.1 made negligible difference: for instance, using 1/ln⁡(1+t+t2)1/\ln(1+t+t^{2}) instead of 1/2​ln⁡(t)1/2\ln(t) with x=1011x=10^{11} gave the estimate 129 297 407.4129\,297\,407.4, compared with 129 297 407.9129\,297\,407.9 in Table 2.) The proportional errors shown are less that 0.000340.00034, that is, 0.034%0.034\%. Similar comparisons for other values of nn and ee were reassuring but less convincing, as the numbers of projective primes within our computing range were much smaller: for example, with n=5n=5 and e=1e=1 we obtained an estimate of 246.718​…246.718\ldots for the number of projective primes p=1+q+⋯+q4<1018p=1+q+\cdots+q^{4}<10^{18}, whereas the correct number is 252. (Note that in order to estimate the number of primes p=1+q+q2≤1018p=1+q+q^{2}\leq 10^{18} we have to compute the integral in (5) up to x=1018/2x=10^{18/2}; however, for p=1+q+⋯+q4<1018p=1+q+\cdots+q^{4}<10^{18} the integral is up to 1018/410^{18/4}, over a much smaller interval.)

On the basis of this evidence, we make the following conjecture:

Conjecture 9.2

There are infinitely many projective primes of the form p=1+q+q2p=1+q+q^{2} where qq is prime.

On the basis of similar evidence for n>3n>3 or e>1e>1, but necessarily involving smaller numbers of projective primes, we make the following more general conjecture:

Conjecture 9.3

For each fixed prime n≥3n\geq 3 and each fixed power ee of nn, there are infinitely many projective primes of the form p=1+q+⋯+qn−1p=1+q+\cdots+q^{n-1} where qq is the ee-th power of a prime.

Of course, rather weaker statements than these would also imply the existence of infinitely many projective primes. For example, it would be sufficient to prove that for infinitely many primes nn (resp. primes power qq) there is at least one prime power qq (resp. prime nn) such that (qn−1)/(q−1)(q^{n}-1)/(q-1) is prime. This would give an infinite set of such pairs (n,q)(n,q), with any specific prime represented by at most finitely many of them.

10 Groups and dessins of projective prime degrees

Returning to the groups, the elements zz of order p=(qn−1)/(q−1)p=(q^{n}-1)/(q-1) in G=PSLn​(q)G={\rm PSL}_{n}(q) are the Singer cycles (see [39, Satz II.7.3], for example), induced by appropriate non-zero elements of 𝔽qn{\mathbb{F}}_{q^{n}} acting linearly by multiplication on that field, regarded as an nn-dimensional vector space over 𝔽q{\mathbb{F}}_{q}, and permuting its 11-dimensional subspaces regularly. It follows from results of Berecky [7] that when a Singer cycle zz has prime order pp the only maximal subgroup of GG containing it is the normaliser NG​(⟨z⟩)≅Cp⋊CnN_{G}(\langle z\rangle)\cong{\rm C}_{p}\rtimes{\rm C}_{n}, where the complement is induced by the Galois group Gal​𝔽qn/𝔽q=⟨t↦tq⟩≅Cn{\rm Gal}\,{\mathbb{F}}_{q^{n}}/{\mathbb{F}}_{q}=\langle t\mapsto t^{q}\rangle\cong{\rm C}_{n}. Being solvable, NG​(⟨z⟩)N_{G}(\langle z\rangle) cannot contain a perfect subgroup ⟨x,y,z⟩\langle x,y,z\rangle, so any triple of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p), if it exists, must generate GG. Moreover, there are (p−1)/n(p-1)/n conjugacy classes 𝒵\mathcal{Z} of Singer cycles zz in GG, one for each orbit of Gal​𝔽qn/𝔽q{\rm Gal}\,{\mathbb{F}}_{q^{n}}/{\mathbb{F}}_{q} on elements of multiplicative order pp in 𝔽qn{\mathbb{F}}_{q^{n}}. (Note that since nn is prime we have p−1=q+q2+⋯+qn−1≡0p-1=q+q^{2}+\cdots+q^{n-1}\equiv 0 mod (n)(n): this is obvious if q≡0q\equiv 0 or 11 mod (n)(n), and otherwise since nn is prime the summands represent the non-zero congruence classes mod (n)(n), so they cancel in pairs.

For the small projective primes p=5p=5, 77, 1313 and 1717 the groups PSL2(4)(≅PSL2(5)≅A5){\rm PSL}_{2}(4)\;(\cong{\rm PSL}_{2}(5)\cong{\rm A}_{5}), PSL3​(2)(≅PSL2​(7)){\rm PSL}_{3}(2)\;(\cong{\rm PSL}_{2}(7)), PSL3​(3){\rm PSL}_{3}(3) and PSL2​(16){\rm PSL}_{2}(16) arise as monodromy groups. We will systematically examine various possibilities for monodromy groups PSLn​(q){\rm PSL}_{n}(q), starting with small values of nn.

10.1 The case n=2n=2: Fermat primes

In the case of the Fermat primes, where n=2n=2, we have the following:

Theorem 10.1

For each Fermat prime p=22k+1≥5p=2^{2^{k}}+1\geq 5 there are 22k−k−12^{2^{k}-k-1} dessins 𝒟\mathcal{D} of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) and degree pp with monodromy group G=PSL2​(22k)G={\rm PSL}_{2}(2^{2^{k}}), acting naturally. They have genus (p−5)/12(p-5)/12, while their regular covers ℛ\mathcal{R}, which are mutually non-isomorphic, have genus p​(p−4)​(p−5)/12p(p-4)(p-5)/12. Dessins 𝒟\mathcal{D} and ℛ\mathcal{R} are both mirror symmetric.

Let G=PSL2​(q)G={\rm PSL}_{2}(q) where q=22k≥4q=2^{2^{k}}\geq 4 and p=q+1p=q+1 is prime. The conjugacy classes 𝒳\mathcal{X} and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} of elements xx and yy of orders 33 and 22 are unique, while there are q/2q/2 classes 𝒵\mathcal{Z} of elements zz of order pp. Since 33 and pp divide q−1q-1 and q+1q+1 respectively, the character table of GG (see [44, §5.5], for example) shows that only the principal character χ=χ1\chi=\chi_{1} has χ⁡(x)​χ​(y)​χ​(z)≠0\chi(x)\chi(y)\chi(z)\neq 0, so for each choice of 𝒵\mathcal{Z} we have a character sum Σ=1\Sigma=1. Since |C⁡(x)|=q−1|C(x)|=q-1, |C⁡(y)|=q|C(y)|=q, |C⁡(z)|=q+1|C(z)|=q+1 and |G|=q⁡(q2−1)|G|=q(q^{2}-1), the number of triples of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) in GG is

q2⋅|G|2|C⁡(x)|⋅|C⁡(y)|⋅|C⁡(z)|⋅Σ=q2⋅|G|.\frac{q}{2}\cdot\frac{|G|^{2}}{|C(x)|\cdot|C(y)|\cdot|C(z)|}\cdot\Sigma=\frac{q}{2}\cdot|G|.

As explained earlier, results of Berecky [7] on Singer cycles imply that each triple generates GG. We have Aut​G≅G⋊Gal​𝔽q≅G⋊C2k{\rm Aut}\,G\cong G\rtimes{\rm Gal}\,{\mathbb{F}}_{q}\cong G\rtimes{\rm C}_{2^{k}}, acting semi-regularly on these triples, so the number of its orbits on them is

q2⋅12k=22k−k−1.\frac{q}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{2^{k}}=2^{2^{k}-k-1}.

This is therefore the number of normal subgroups of Δ=Δ⁡(3,2,p)\Delta=\Delta(3,2,p) with quotient group GG, and thus the number of regular dessins ℛ\mathcal{R} of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) with automorphism group GG.

Now GG has a unique conjugacy class of subgroups of index p=q+1p=q+1, the stabilisers of points in ℙ1​(𝔽q){\mathbb{P}}^{1}({\mathbb{F}}_{q}). These lift back to 22k−k−12^{2^{k}-k-1} conjugacy classes of subgroups of the same index in Δ\Delta, so they correspond to that number of dessins 𝒟\mathcal{D} of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) and degree pp with monodromy group GG and regular cover one of the dessins ℛ\mathcal{R}. Since xx, yy and zz have cycle structures 3(q−1)/3​123^{(q-1)/3}1^{2}, 2q/2​112^{q/2}1^{1} and p1p^{1} on ℙ1​(𝔽q){\mathbb{P}}^{1}({\mathbb{F}}_{q}), the dessins 𝒟\mathcal{D} have characteristic

χ=q−13+2+q2+1−(q+1)+1=16−q6\chi=\frac{q-1}{3}+2+\frac{q}{2}+1-(q+1)+1=\frac{16-q}{6}

and hence have genus

g=1−χ2=q−412=p−512.g=1-\frac{\chi}{2}=\frac{q-4}{12}=\frac{p-5}{12}.

By the Riemann–Hurwitz formula the regular dessins ℛ\mathcal{R} have genus

p−612​p​|G|+1=p​(p−4)​(p−5)12.\frac{p-6}{12p}|G|+1=\frac{p(p-4)(p-5)}{12}.

Each of the conjugacy classes 𝒵\mathcal{Z} consists of mutually inverse pairs z,zq=z−1z,z^{q}=z^{-1}, so the maps 𝒟\mathcal{D} and ℛ\mathcal{R} are isomorphic to their mirror images. (In fact, as noted by Singerman [70], it follows from results of Macbeath [58] that for any prime power qq, each generating pair for PSL2​(q){\rm PSL}_{2}(q) are simultaneously inverted by an automorphism, implying this result more generally.)

Example 10.2

If k=1k=1 and p=5p=5 we obtain one planar dessin 𝒟\mathcal{D}, shown on the left in Figure 11, with monodromy group G=PSL2​(4)≅A5G={\rm PSL}_{2}(4)\cong{\rm A}_{5}; its regular cover ℛ\mathcal{R} is the dodecahedron, and 𝒟\mathcal{D} is the quotient of ℛ\mathcal{R} by a point-stabiliser in GG, isomorphic to A4{\rm A}_{4}. If k=2k=2 and p=17p=17 we obtain two dessins of genus 11; they are shown in Section 14, Figure 25. Their regular covers are of genus 221221. If k=3k=3 and p=257p=257 we obtain 1616 dessins of genus 2121, with regular covers of genus 1 365 4411\,365\,441. If k=4k=4 and p=65 537p=65\,537 we obtain 20482048 dessins of genus 54615461, with regular covers of genus 23 454 100 602 88123\,454\,100\,602\,881. No Fermat primes are known for k≥5k\geq 5, and it is conjectured that none exist, but if any do, they are covered by Theorem 10.1.

Having dealt with the case n=2n=2, we will now assume that n≥3n\geq 3. In this case PSLn​(q){\rm PSL}_{n}(q) has two natural representations, on points and hyperplanes of ℙn−1​(𝔽q){\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}({\mathbb{F}}_{q}), transposed by the outer automorphism induced by the duality of this geometry. Another difference between this case and the case n=2n=2 is that when n≥3n\geq 3 the conjugacy classes 𝒵\mathcal{Z} of Singer cycles are not inverse closed: instead, they form mutually inverse pairs of classes, transposed by duality. This implies that the dessins 𝒟\mathcal{D} occur in chiral pairs, each pair having the same regular cover ℛ\mathcal{R}, which is regular as a map, that is, isomorphic to its mirror image.

10.2 The case n=3n=3: projective planes

The great majority of projective primes, up to a given bound, have n=3n=3, so that the group G=PSL3​(q)G={\rm PSL}_{3}(q) acts on the points and lines of the projective plane ℙ2​(𝔽q){\mathbb{P}}^{2}({\mathbb{F}}_{q}). In this case one can enumerate and describe the associated dessins by using the generic character table for GG given by Simpson and Frame in [69], in addition to those in the ATLAS [17] for q≤9q\leq 9.

Theorem 10.3

If qq is a prime power such that p:=1+q+q2p:=1+q+q^{2} is prime, there are (p−1)/3​e(p-1)/3e dessins of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) and degree pp with monodromy group PSL3​(q){\rm PSL}_{3}(q) acting naturally, where qq is the ee-th power of a prime. They are all chiral. If qq is odd they have passport (3q⁡(q+1)/3​11,2(q2−1)/2​1q+2,p1)(3^{q(q+1)/3}1^{1},2^{(q^{2}-1)/2}1^{q+2},p^{1}) and genus (q−3)​(q+1)/12(q-3)(q+1)/12, whereas if q=2eq=2^{e} their passport is (3q⁡(q+1)/3​11,2q2/2​1q+1,p1)(3^{q(q+1)/3}1^{1},2^{q^{2}/2}1^{q+1},p^{1}) and their genus is q⁡(q−2)/12q(q-2)/12.

Let G:=PSL3​(q)G:={\rm PSL}_{3}(q). By Lemma 8.5(c) we have G=SL3​(q)G={\rm SL}_{3}(q). We will apply the Frobenius formula (2) to GG, using the generic character table for SL3​(q){\rm SL}_{3}(q) in [69, Table 1b].

First assume that qq is coprime to 66. There are unique conjugacy classes 𝒳\mathcal{X} and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} of elements of order 33 and 22 in GG, and there are (p−1)/3=q⁡(q+1)/3(p-1)/3=q(q+1)/3 classes 𝒵\mathcal{Z} of elements (Singer cycles) of order pp; these classes have types 𝒞7{\mathcal{C}}_{7}, 𝒞4{\mathcal{C}}_{4} and 𝒞8{\mathcal{C}}_{8} in the notation of [69, Table 1a], and their elements have centralisers of orders q2−1q^{2}-1, q​(q−1)2​(q+1)q(q-1)^{2}(q+1) and pp. The only non-principal irreducible character of GG which does not vanish on 𝒳{\mathcal{X}}, 𝒴{\mathcal{Y}} or 𝒵{\mathcal{Z}} is the Steinberg character, the unique irreducible character of degree q3q^{3}, which takes the values −1-1, qq and 11 on them. Since |G|=q3​(q−1)2​(q+1)​(q2+q+1)|G|=q^{3}(q-1)^{2}(q+1)(q^{2}+q+1) we find that the number of triples of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) in GG is

p−13⋅(q3​(q−1)2​(q+1)​(q2+q+1))2(q2−1)⋅q​(q−1)2​(q+1)⋅p​(1+(−1)⋅q⋅1q3)=p−13​|G|.\frac{p-1}{3}\cdot\frac{(q^{3}(q-1)^{2}(q+1)(q^{2}+q+1))^{2}}{(q^{2}-1)\cdot q(q-1)^{2}(q+1)\cdot p}\left(1+\frac{(-1)\cdot q\cdot 1}{q^{3}}\right)=\frac{p-1}{3}|G|.

By [7] the only maximal subgroup of GG containing zz is NG​(⟨z⟩)N_{G}(\langle z\rangle), of order 3​p3p, so any such triple generates GG. If qq is the ee-th power of a prime then |Out​G|=2​e|{\rm Out}\,G|=2e, the two factors corresponding to duality of the projective plane ℙ2​(𝔽q){\mathbb{P}}^{2}({\mathbb{F}}_{q}) on which GG acts and the Galois group of 𝔽q{\mathbb{F}}_{q}, so Δ⁡(3,2,p)\Delta(3,2,p) has (p−1)/6​e(p-1)/6e normal subgroups with quotient GG. Since GG has two conjugacy classes of subgroups of index pp, the stabilisers of points and lines in ℙ2​(𝔽q){\mathbb{P}}^{2}({\mathbb{F}}_{q}), we obtain (p−1)/3​e(p-1)/3e dessins of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) and degree pp with monodromy group GG.

In each of the two actions of degree pp of GG, the elements xx, yy and zz fix 11, q+2q+2 and 00 points, so these dessins all have passport (3q⁡(q+1)/3​11,2(q2−1)/2​1q+2,p1)(3^{q(q+1)/3}1^{1},2^{(q^{2}-1)/2}1^{q+2},p^{1}) and hence genus (q−3)​(q+1)/12(q-3)(q+1)/12.

If q=3eq=3^{e} there are two conjugacy classes of elements of order 33, of types 𝒞2{\mathcal{C}}_{2} and 𝒞3{\mathcal{C}}_{3}, with centralisers of order q3​(q−1)q^{3}(q-1) and q2q^{2}. If xx is chosen from the first class, then only the principal character and the constituent of the permutation character of degree p−1=q⁡(q+1)p-1=q(q+1) contribute to the character sum Σ\Sigma, and this sum is equal to

Σ=1+q⋅(q+1)⋅(−1)q⁡(q+1)=0.\Sigma=1+\frac{q\cdot(q+1)\cdot(-1)}{q(q+1)}=0.

If xx is chosen from the second class, then only the principal character contributes to Σ\Sigma, so the resulting number of triples in GG is

p−13⋅(q3​(q−1)2​(q+1)​(q2+q+1))2q2⋅q​(q−1)2​(q+1)⋅p=p−13​|G|\frac{p-1}{3}\cdot\frac{(q^{3}(q-1)^{2}(q+1)(q^{2}+q+1))^{2}}{q^{2}\cdot q(q-1)^{2}(q+1)\cdot p}=\frac{p-1}{3}|G|

as before. The number of dessins is therefore again (p−1)/3​e(p-1)/3e, and the passport and genus are also as before.

If q=2eq=2^{e} then the main changes are that the unique class 𝒴\mathcal{Y} of involutions has type 𝒞2{\mathcal{C}}_{2}, with centralisers of order q3​(q−1)q^{3}(q-1), and that every non-principal irreducible character vanishes on xx, yy or zz, so Σ=1\Sigma=1. The number of triples of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) in GG is therefore

p−13⋅(q3​(q−1)2​(q+1)​(q2+q+1))2(q2−1)⋅q3​(q−1)⋅p=p−13​|G|,\frac{p-1}{3}\cdot\frac{(q^{3}(q-1)^{2}(q+1)(q^{2}+q+1))^{2}}{(q^{2}-1)\cdot q^{3}(q-1)\cdot p}=\frac{p-1}{3}|G|,

so the number of dessins is again (p−1)/3​e(p-1)/3e. The other change is that yy now fixes q+1q+1 points, so that the passport is (3q⁡(q+1)/3​11,2q2/2​1q+1,p1)(3^{q(q+1)/3}1^{1},2^{q^{2}/2}1^{q+1},p^{1}) and the genus is q⁡(q−2)/12q(q-2)/12.

In all cases, chirality of the dessins follows from the facts that the two dual representations of GG of degree pp correspond to a mutually inverse pair of conjugacy classes 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, and that Out​G{\rm Out}\,G acts semiregularly on the set of such pairs.

Example 10.4

The smallest example for the above theorem is the chiral pair of dessins of degree p=7p=7 with monodromy group PSL3​(2)≅PSL2​(7){\rm PSL}_{3}(2)\cong{\rm PSL}_{2}(7); one of this pair is shown on the right in Figure 11.

Example 10.5

Let p=13p=13 and G=PSL3​(3)G={\rm PSL}_{3}(3). The required conjugacy classes are (in ATLAS [17] notation) 𝒳=3​B{\mathcal{X}}=3B, 𝒴=2​A{\mathcal{Y}}=2A and 𝒵=13​A,13​B,13​C{\mathcal{Z}}=13A,13B,13C or 13​D13D, giving four dessins 𝒟\mathcal{D} of type (3,2,13)(3,2,13) and degree 1313; they form two chiral pairs, each pair having the same regular cover. Each dessin 𝒟\mathcal{D} (see Figure 12, or [1, Orbit 13.1, Fig. 8.22(A)]) has passport (34​11,24​15,131)(3^{4}1^{1},2^{4}1^{5},13^{1}) and genus 00, while the two regular covers have genus 253253. (These are the duals of the regular maps R253.1 and R253.2 of type {3,13}8\{3,13\}_{8} and {3,13}12\{3,13\}_{12} in [16].)

Example 10.6

Let p=31p=31, with G=PSL3​(5)G={\rm PSL}_{3}(5). In this case 𝒳=3​A{\mathcal{X}}=3A, 𝒴=2​A{\mathcal{Y}}=2A and there are ten possible classes 𝒵=31​A,31​B,…{\mathcal{Z}}=31A,31B,\ldots. These give ten dessins 𝒟\mathcal{D} of type (3,2,31)(3,2,31) and degree 3131, forming five chiral pairs with five regular covers. Each dessin 𝒟\mathcal{D} has passport (310​11,212​17,311)(3^{10}1^{1},2^{12}1^{7},31^{1}) and genus 11, while the regular covers have genus 25 00125\,001. Generators of the monodromy groups of these ten dessins 𝒟\mathcal{D}, as well as the diagram of one of them, are given in Subsection 14.4.

Example 10.7

Let p=73p=73 and G=PSL3​(8)G={\rm PSL}_{3}(8). Here 𝒳=3​A{\mathcal{X}}=3A and 𝒴=2​A{\mathcal{Y}}=2A, and there are 2424 classes 𝒵=73​A,…{\mathcal{Z}}=73A,\ldots of elements of order 7373. Since e=3e=3 we obtain 24/3=824/3=8 dessins 𝒟\mathcal{D}. They have passport (324​11,232​19,731)(3^{24}1^{1},2^{32}1^{9},73^{1}) and genus 44; their permutation representations are given in Subsection 14.7. They form four chiral pairs, each pair having a regular cover of genus 1 260 6731\,260\,673.

Of course, we do not consider cases such as q=4q=4, 77, 99 and 1111 since the corresponding values of 1+q+q21+q+q^{2} are not prime. Indeed, squares of primes can be ignored, since for pp to be prime we require ee to be a power of n=3n=3. For any such ee, the Bateman–Horn conjecture, applied to the polynomials tt and 1+te+t2​e1+t^{e}+t^{2e}, suggests that infinitely many projective primes will be obtained. However, even for e=3e=3 there are so few examples within our computing range (1010 primes p=1+q+q2<1018p=1+q+q^{2}<10^{18}, compared with an estimate of about 1212) that the computational evidence is not convincing.

10.3 Fixed n>3n>3

In the case of a prime n>3n>3 we do not have generic character tables for PSLn​(q){\rm PSL}_{n}(q). Nevertheless, the Bateman–Horn Conjecture still applies, again suggesting that if we fix nn and take ee to be a fixed power of nn we will obtain infinitely many projective primes. The only case in which the computational evidence is persuasive is when n=5n=5 and e=1e=1, with 252252 projective primes p<1018p<10^{18}, compared with an estimate of about 246246.

10.4 The case q=2q=2: Mersenne primes

When q=2q=2 we have G=PSLn​(2)=GLn​(2)G={\rm PSL}_{n}(2)={\rm GL}_{n}(2), and p=2n−1p=2^{n}-1, currently known to be prime for 5151 values of nn. No generic character tables for GLn​(2){\rm GL}_{n}(2) are available, although there is a general theory of characters for GLn​(q){\rm GL}_{n}(q), largely based on the work of Green [34]; for a concise and readable summary, see [56, §4] or [59, Ch. IV]. Here are two small examples where character tables in [17] can be used.

Example 10.8

Let p=23−1=7p=2^{3}-1=7 and G=PSL3(2)(=GL3(2)≅PSL2(7))G={\rm PSL}_{3}(2)\;(={\rm GL}_{3}(2)\cong{\rm PSL}_{2}(7)). The only conjugacy classes of elements of order 33 or 22 in GG are 3​A3A and 2​A2A, with cycle structures 32​113^{2}1^{1} and 22​132^{2}1^{3} in both of the natural representations of GG, on points and lines of the Fano plane ℙ2​(𝔽2){\mathbb{P}}^{2}({\mathbb{F}}_{2}); there are two classes 7​A,7​B7A,7B of elements of order p=7p=7. The only character which does not vanish in the character sum is χ1\chi_{1}, so Σ=1\Sigma=1. Since |C⁡(x)|=3|C(x)|=3, |C⁡(y)|=8=23|C(y)|=8=2^{3}, |C⁡(z)|=7|C(z)|=7 and |G|=168=23⋅3⋅7|G|=168=2^{3}\cdot 3\cdot 7, the number of triples of type (3,2,7)(3,2,7) in GG is

2⋅26⋅32⋅723⋅23⋅7=24⋅3⋅7=2​|G|=|Aut​G|.2\cdot\frac{2^{6}\cdot 3^{2}\cdot 7^{2}}{3\cdot 2^{3}\cdot 7}=2^{4}\cdot 3\cdot 7=2|G|=|{\rm Aut}\,G|.

(Note that Out​G≅C2{\rm Out}\,G\cong{\rm C}_{2}, induced by the duality of the Fano plane, or equivalently by conjugation of PSL2​(7){\rm PSL}_{2}(7) in PGL2​(7){\rm PGL}_{2}(7).) These triples all generate GG, so Δ=Δ⁡(3,2,7)\Delta=\Delta(3,2,7) has a unique normal subgroup with quotient GG, corresponding to a regular dessin ℛ\mathcal{R} of type (3,2,7)(3,2,7) with automorphism group GG. There are two conjugacy classes of subgroups of index 77 in GG, the stabilisers of points and lines in the Fano plane; these lift to two conjugacy classes of subgroups of index 77 in Δ\Delta, corresponding to two dessins 𝒟\mathcal{D} of type (3,2,7)(3,2,7) and degree 77, each having regular cover ℛ\mathcal{R}. Each dessin 𝒟\mathcal{D} has passport (32​11,22​13,71)(3^{2}1^{1},2^{2}1^{3},7^{1}), so it has genus 00, while ℛ\mathcal{R} has genus 33. One of the two dessins 𝒟\mathcal{D} is shown on the right in Figure 11, and the other is its mirror image 𝒟¯\overline{\mathcal{D}}. These two maps, corresponding to the two choices for the conjugacy class 𝒵\mathcal{Z} or to the two choices for the class of subgroups of index 77, are not isomorphic since the outer automorphism of GG transposes both pairs. The dessin ℛ\mathcal{R} is Klein’s heptagonal map on his quartic curve, introduced in [50]; it is denoted by {7,3}8\{7,3\}_{8} in [20] and is the dual of R3.1 in [16]. As the common regular cover of a chiral pair of dessins (or by its uniqueness) this map is isomorphic to its mirror image.

Example 10.9

Let p=31p=31 (again), but now in its role as a Mersenne prime 25−12^{5}-1, with G=PSL5​(2)=GL5​(2)G={\rm PSL}_{5}(2)={\rm GL}_{5}(2). There are two classes each of elements of orders 33 and 22, namely 3​A3A and 3​B3B, with cycle structures 38​173^{8}1^{7} and 310​113^{10}1^{1}, and 2​A2A and 2​B2B, with cycle structures 28​1152^{8}1^{15} and 212​172^{12}1^{7}, together with six classes 31​A,…31A,\ldots of elements of order 3131. The inequality 2​a+b≥p−12a+b\geq p-1 discussed earlier implies that 𝒳\mathcal{X} and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} must be 3​B3B and 2​B2B. For each of the six choices of 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, only χ1\chi_{1} and χ6\chi_{6} appear in the character sum, so

Σ=1+8⋅(−5)⋅1280=1−17=67.\Sigma=1+\frac{8\cdot(-5)\cdot 1}{280}=1-\frac{1}{7}=\frac{6}{7}.

We have |C⁡(x)|=180=22⋅32⋅5|C(x)|=180=2^{2}\cdot 3^{2}\cdot 5, |C⁡(y)|=1536=29⋅3|C(y)|=1536=2^{9}\cdot 3, |C⁡(z)|=31|C(z)|=31 and |G|=9 999 360=210⋅32⋅5⋅7⋅31|G|=9\,999\,360=2^{10}\cdot 3^{2}\cdot 5\cdot 7\cdot 31, so the total number of triples in GG is

6⋅29⋅3⋅5⋅72⋅31⋅67=211⋅33⋅5⋅7⋅31=6​|G|=3​|Aut​G|.6\cdot 2^{9}\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 7^{2}\cdot 31\cdot\frac{6}{7}=2^{11}\cdot 3^{3}\cdot 5\cdot 7\cdot 31=6|G|=3|{\rm Aut}\,G|.

Each triple generates GG, so Δ\Delta has three normal subgroups with quotient GG. There are two conjugacy classes of subgroups of index 3131 in GG, the stabilisers of points and hyperplanes in ℙ4​(𝔽2){\mathbb{P}}^{4}({\mathbb{F}}_{2}), giving six dessins 𝒟\mathcal{D} of degree 3131, with three chiral pairs each having the same regular cover ℛ\mathcal{R}. Each dessin 𝒟\mathcal{D} has passport (310​11,212​17,311)(3^{10}1^{1},2^{12}1^{7},31^{1}), so it has genus 11, while the regular covers ℛ\mathcal{R} have genus 672 001672\,001. Generators of the monodromy groups of these six dessins 𝒟\mathcal{D}, as well as the diagram of one of them, are given in Subsection 14.5.

Remark 10.10 (Goormaghtigh conjecture)

Note that 3131 appears twice as a projective prime, as both 1+5+521+5+5^{2} and 1+2+22+23+241+2+2^{2}+2^{3}+2^{4}. In 1917 Goormaghtigh [32] conjectured that this example and 1+2+22+⋯+212=8191=1+90+9021+2+2^{2}+\cdots+2^{12}=8191=1+90+90^{2} are the only repetitions among numbers of the form (qn−1)/(q−1)(q^{n}-1)/(q-1) for integers q,n≥2q,n\geq 2. Although 81918191 is prime (and hence a projective prime for (q,n)=(2,13)(q,n)=(2,13)), 9090 is not a prime power, so only the first example is a repetition of projective primes. A computer search of prime degrees up to 101810^{18} has revealed no further examples. The conjecture is still open. For additional information see [33].

Before attempting to find triples (x,y,z)(x,y,z) of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) in G=GLn​(2)G={\rm GL}_{n}(2) for general primes n≥3n\geq 3, it is useful first to consider the possibilities for elements of orders 33, 22 and pp in GG. Any element x∈Gx\in G of order 33 has a rational canonical form with rr and (n−r)/2(n-r)/2 blocks of the form

(1)or(0111)\left(\,\begin{array}[]{c}1\\ \end{array}\,\right)\quad{\rm or}\quad\left(\,\begin{array}[]{cc}0&1\\ 1&1\\ \end{array}\right)

for some odd r<nr<n, so it fixes a subspace of ℙn−1​(𝔽2){\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}({\mathbb{F}}_{2}) of dimension r−1r-1; this contains α=2r−1\alpha=2^{r}-1 points, so xx has a=(p−2r+1)/3a=(p-2^{r}+1)/3 nontrivial cycles. Similarly, any element y∈Gy\in G of order 22 has a Jordan normal form with ss and (n−s)/2(n-s)/2 blocks of the form

(1)or(1101)\left(\,\begin{array}[]{c}1\\ \end{array}\,\right)\quad{\rm or}\quad\left(\,\begin{array}[]{cc}1&1\\ 0&1\\ \end{array}\right)

for some odd s<ns<n; it therefore fixes a subspace of dimension (n+s−2)/2(n+s-2)/2 containing β=2(n+s)/2−1\beta=2^{(n+s)/2}-1 points, so it has b=(p−2(n+s)/2+1)/2b=(p-2^{(n+s)/2}+1)/2 nontrivial cycles. The element zz is a pp-cycle, so provided a triple (x,y,z)(x,y,z) of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) exists, it will generate GG by [7]; the resulting dessin 𝒟\mathcal{D} will have passport (3a​1α,2b​1β,p1)(3^{a}1^{\alpha},2^{b}1^{\beta},p^{1}) and genus (2​a+b+1−p)/2(2a+b+1-p)/2, while its minimal regular cover ℛ\mathcal{R} will have genus

p−612​p​|G|+1=p−612​p​∏i=0n−1(2n−2i)+1=(p−6)​2(n2−n−4)/2​∏i=3n−1(2i−1)+1,\frac{p-6}{12p}|G|+1=\frac{p-6}{12p}\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(2^{n}-2^{i})+1=(p-6)2^{(n^{2}-n-4)/2}\prod_{i=3}^{n-1}(2^{i}-1)+1,

independent of rr and ss. In particular, if we choose the most ‘active’ elements xx and yy by taking r=s=1r=s=1 (as in the earlier examples with n=3n=3 and 55) we will have α=1\alpha=1 and β=2(n+1)/2−1\beta=2^{(n+1)/2}-1, so a=(p−1)/3a=(p-1)/3 and b=(p−2(n+1)/2+1)/2b=(p-2^{(n+1)/2}+1)/2 and hence 𝒟\mathcal{D} will have genus

13​(2n−2+1)−2(n−3)/2.\frac{1}{3}(2^{n-2}+1)-2^{(n-3)/2}. (7)
Theorem 10.11

For each Mersenne prime p=2n−1≥7p=2^{n}-1\geq 7 there are at least (p−1)/2​n(p-1)/2n chiral pairs of dessins of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p), degree pp and genus given by (7), with monodromy group G=PSLn​(2)=GLn​(2)G={\rm PSL}_{n}(2)={\rm GL}_{n}(2).

Proof. We will use the Frobenius formula (2) to show that for each conjugacy class 𝒵\mathcal{Z} of Singer cycles in GG there a triple (x,y,z)(x,y,z) of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) where xx and yy satisfy r=s=1r=s=1 (as above) and z∈𝒵z\in{\mathcal{Z}}. The calculation is aided by the fact that most of the non-principal irreducible characters of GG vanish on the Singer cycles zz (see [56, §4.2], for example), and hence do not contribute to the character sum Σ\Sigma. Among the other characters, that of degree p−1p-1, the non-principal constituent of the natural permutation character, vanishes on xx, while the Steinberg character of degree 2n⁡(n−1)/22^{n(n-1)/2} vanishes on yy, so they can also be ignored. The remaining characters have sufficiently large degrees, compared with their values at x,yx,y and zz (see [56, §4.1,4.2] for full details), that their total contribution to Σ\Sigma has modulus less than the contribution 11 of the principal character, so that Σ>0\Sigma>0 and hence the required triples exist. As before, they all generate GG by [7]. There are (p−1)/n(p-1)/n conjugacy classes 𝒵\mathcal{Z} of Singer cycles zz in GG, forming (p−1)/2​n(p-1)/2n mutually inverse pairs; each pair are transposed by the outer automorphism group of GG, as are the two permutation representations of GG of degree pp; thus we obtain (at least) (p−1)/2​n(p-1)/2n chiral pairs of dessins 𝒟\mathcal{D}, all with the same passport and genus, as calculated above. □\square

On the basis of Theorem 10.11, and of other examples involving small projective primes, we conjecture the following extension of this theorem:

Conjecture 10.12

For each projective prime p=1+q+⋯+qn−1>3p=1+q+\cdots+q^{n-1}>3 there exists at least one dessin of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) and degree pp with monodromy group PSLn​(q){\rm PSL}_{n}(q).

10.5 Summary

We can summarise the results of this rather long section as follows:

Theorem 10.13

Suppose that pp is a prime such that there is a dessin of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) and degree pp with monodromy group GG. Then p≥5p\geq 5, and one of the following holds:

  • (a)

    G=ApG={\rm A}_{p}, acting naturally, with p≠7p\neq 7;

  • (b)

    p=11p=11 and G=PSL2​(p)G={\rm PSL}_{2}(p), acting on the cosets of a subgroup isomorphic to A5{\rm A}_{5};

  • (c)

    pp is a projective prime (qn−1)/(q−1)(q^{n}-1)/(q-1) for some prime nn and prime-power qq, and G=PSLn​(q)=SLn​(q)G={\rm PSL}_{n}(q)={\rm SL}_{n}(q) acting naturally on points or hyperplanes of ℙn−1​(q){\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}(q).

In case (a), if p=5p=5 there is a unique dessin, shown on the left in Figure 11; if p>7p>7 there are exponentially many dessins as p→∞p\to\infty, even if we restrict to planar dessins. In case (b) there is a single chiral pair of dessins; these are the dessins ℳ1{\mathcal{M}}_{1} and ℳ¯1\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1} studied by Klein in [51] and shown in Figures 2 and  3. In case (c) we conjecture that there are infinitely many projective primes pp, even for any fixed prime n≥3n\geq 3; when n=2n=2 (Fermat primes) or 33 (projective planes) the dessins are all as described in Theorem 10.1 or Theorem 10.3. In the case q=2q=2 (Mersenne primes) we have an existence result rather than a complete classification.

11 Modular dessins and curves

Just as we generalised our arguments about dessins of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) and degree pp from p=11p=11 to all primes pp, we can do the same for dessins of this type and of degree p+1p+1. In this section we will consider the dessins 𝒟0​(p){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(p) arising naturally from congruence subgroups of level pp in the modular group, and in the next section we will consider more general dessins of this type and degree.

11.1 𝒟0​(p){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(p) and its passport

As in the case p=11p=11 considered earlier, for any prime pp the natural action of PSL2​(p){\rm PSL}_{2}(p) on the projective line ℙ1​(𝔽p){\mathbb{P}}^{1}({\mathbb{F}}_{p}) yields a dessin 𝒟0​(p){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(p) of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) and degree p+1p+1. One can find its passport by using the fact that a non-identity Möbius transformation (over any field) has at most two fixed points. The cases p=2p=2 and 33 are trivial, so let us assume that p≥5p\geq 5.

The permutation xx representing the black vertices has order 33, so

  • •

    if p≡1p\equiv 1 mod (3)(3) then xx has two fixed points, and its cycle type is 3(p−1)/3​123^{(p-1)/3}1^{2};

  • •

    if p≡−1p\equiv-1 mod (3)(3) then xx has no fixed points, and its cycle type is 3(p+1)/33^{(p+1)/3}.

Similarly the permutation yy representing the white vertices has order 22, and is even, so

  • •

    if p≡1p\equiv 1 mod (4)(4) then yy has two fixed points, and its cycle structure is 2(p−1)/2​122^{(p-1)/2}1^{2};

  • •

    if p≡−1p\equiv-1 mod (4)(4) then yy has no fixed points, and its cycle structure is 2(p+1)/22^{(p+1)/2}.

Finally the permutation zz representing the faces has order pp, so its cycle structure is p1​11p^{1}1^{1}.

From the passport one can compute the Euler characteristic χ\chi and hence the genus gg of 𝒟0​(p){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(p). There are four cases:

  • •

    if p≡1p\equiv 1 mod (12)(12) the passport is (3(p−1)/3​12,2(p−1)/2​12,p1​11)(3^{(p-1)/3}1^{2},2^{(p-1)/2}1^{2},p^{1}1^{1}), giving the genus g=(p−13)/12g=(p-13)/12;

  • •

    if p≡5p\equiv 5 mod (12)(12) the passport is (3(p+1)/3,2(p−1)/2​12,p1​11)(3^{(p+1)/3},2^{(p-1)/2}1^{2},p^{1}1^{1}), giving the genus g=(p−5)/12g=(p-5)/12;

  • •

    if p≡7p\equiv 7 mod (12)(12) the passport is (3(p−1)/3​12,2(p+1)/2,p1​11)(3^{(p-1)/3}1^{2},2^{(p+1)/2},p^{1}1^{1}), giving the genus g=(p−7)/12g=(p-7)/12;

  • •

    if p≡11p\equiv 11 mod (12)(12) the passport is (3(p+1)/3,2(p+1)/2,p1​11)(3^{(p+1)/3},2^{(p+1)/2},p^{1}1^{1}), giving the genus g=(p+1)/12g=(p+1)/12;

Thus the genus of 𝒟0​(p){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(p) is (p−c)/12(p-c)/12 for primes p≡c=−1,5,7p\equiv c=-1,5,7 or 1313 mod (12)(12), and 00 for p=2p=2 or 33. Table 3 gives the values of gg for the first few primes. Figure 13 shows the planar dessins from this table.

11.2 The dessin 𝒟0​(13){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(13)

The dessin 𝒟0​(p){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(p) is planar if and only if p=2,3,5,7p=2,3,5,7 or 1313. These five dessins are shown in Figure 13. It is easy to see that the first four are uniquely determined by their passports, and the same applies to the torus dessin 𝒟0​(11){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(11) which we will show in Figure 17. However, for p=13p=13 there are 30 dessins with passport (34​12,26​12,p1​11)(3^{4}1^{2},2^{6}1^{2},p^{1}1^{1}), consisting of two mirror symmetric dessins, including 𝒟0​(13){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(13), and 14 chiral pairs. In fact, a simple argument shows that these dessins can all be formed from the three basic maps in Figure 14, together with the mirror images of the first and last, by adding black vertices to two of their four free edges. This gives 5×(42)=30\displaystyle 5\times\left(\!\!\begin{array}[]{c}4\\ 2\end{array}\!\!\right)=30 dessins.

Whereas 𝒟0​(13){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(13) has monodromy group PSL2​(13){\rm PSL}_{2}(13), the other 2929 dessins all have monodromy group A14{\rm A}_{14}; this follows from the fact that such a group must be a doubly transitive subgroup of A14{\rm A}_{14}, and apart from A14{\rm}A_{14} itself the only other possibility is PSL2​(13){\rm PSL}_{2}(13), which by the Frobenius formula corresponds to just one dessin, namely 𝒟0​(13){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(13).

The fact that 𝒟0​(13){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(13) is planar gives us some hope of computing its Belyĭ function f:Σ→Σf:\Sigma\to\Sigma, which is as follows:

f=−11728⋅(t4−7​t3+20​t2−19​t+1)3​(t2−5​t+13)t,f=-\frac{1}{1728}\cdot\frac{(t^{4}-7t^{3}+20t^{2}-19t+1)^{3}(t^{2}-5t+13)}{t},
f−1=−11728⋅(t6−10​t5+46​t4−108​t3+122​t2−38​t−1)2​(t2−6​t+13)t.f-1=-\frac{1}{1728}\cdot\frac{(t^{6}-10t^{5}+46t^{4}-108t^{3}+122t^{2}-38t-1)^{2}(t^{2}-6t+13)}{t}.

In this case, of course, ff is not a polynomial, since there is a pole at 00 (the face-centre enclosed by the loop) in addition to the pole at ∞\infty (the centre of the outer face).

Figure 15 shows a geometrically correct version of 𝒟0​(13){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(13), with black and white vertices. In this picture, the loop is so small that it is obscured by its incident black and white vertices. (We will meet a similar problem for 𝒟0​(11){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(11) in Figure 18.) Figure 16 shows a magnified drawing of the loop, together with nearby parts of the real and imaginary axes.

11.3 The dessin 𝒟0​(11){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(11)

Whereas 𝒟0​(p){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(p) is planar for each prime p≤13p\leq 13 except 1111, the dessin 𝒟0​(11){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(11) has genus 11, so we have the additional problem of determining the corresponding elliptic curve. Two views of this dessin are shown in Figure 17 as maps on a torus, with opposite sides of the outer square or hexagon identified in the usual way. Like the dessins ℳ1{\mathcal{M}}_{1} and ℳ¯1\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1}, 𝒟0​(11){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(11) has the dessin ℛ1\mathcal{R}_{1} as its minimal regular cover. However, in this case it is the quotient of ℛ1\mathcal{R}_{1} by the subgroup of L=PSL2​(11)L\,={\rm PSL}_{2}(11) fixing a point in ℙ1​(𝔽11){\mathbb{P}}^{1}({\mathbb{F}}_{11}), of the form C11⋊C5{\rm C}_{11}\rtimes{\rm C}_{5} rather than A5{\rm A}_{5}. In addition to coming from a more natural representation of LL, 𝒟0​(11){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(11) is also more pleasing because of its greater uniformity: the permutations xx and yy have no fixed points, so the black vertices all have valency 33 and there are no free edges. Moreover, the generators y:t↦−1/ty:t\mapsto-1/t and z:t↦t+1z:t\mapsto t+1 of LL can both be seen from the edges and faces through the labelling of directed edges with elements of ℙ1​(𝔽11){\mathbb{P}}^{1}({\mathbb{F}}_{11}). Since x​y​z=1xyz=1, the permutation xx can now easily be computed as x:t↦−1/(t−1)x:t\mapsto-1/(t-1).

Another remarkable feature of this dessin is the fact that it is unique for its passport, which is (34,26,111​11)(3^{4},2^{6},11^{1}1^{1}). One does not have to consider ten different trees and sort out the corresponding groups. We may wonder why Klein overlooked this example. Maybe the reason was that the representation of maps via permutations was not yet invented. The first publications which introduced this construction, by Dyck [24] (1888) and Heffter [38] (1891), appeared only a decade after Klein’s paper. In fact, the pioneer in this subject was Hamilton [37] (1856), but he explained the construction in a private letter. Even at the time close to ours, when the permutational model of maps became a part of a common knowledge, the researchers studied mainly the automorphism groups of maps while their monodromy groups were largely neglected. Only with the advent of the theory of dessins d’enfants the monodromy groups rose to the fore since they are Galois invariants.

From the point of view of dessins d’enfants, the uniqueness of the dessin 𝒟0​(11){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(11) implies that it is defined over ℚ\mathbb{Q}. However, a difficulty of a different sort appears. While in the planar case what we need is a Belyĭ function, which is a rational function f:Σ→Σf:\Sigma\to\Sigma, in the case of a dessin of genus g≥1g\geq 1 we need a Belyĭ pair (X,f)(X,f) where XX is a Riemann surface (or an algebraic curve) of genus gg, and ff is a meromorphic function f:X→Σf:X\to\Sigma with no critical values outside {0,1,∞}\{0,1,\infty\}. There are uncountably many curves of any given genus g≥1g\geq 1, and the dessin determines one of them in a unique way. To find such a curve (and a Belyĭ function defined on it) is an incredibly difficult task. A relatively simple answer below hides numerous obstacles one has to surmount in order to find it. The corresponding computation was made for us by John Voight, to whom we are greatly indebted.

In our case g=1g=1, so the curve in question is an elliptic curve EE. One possible presentation is

y2+y=x3−x2−10​x−20.\displaystyle y^{2}+y=x^{3}-x^{2}-10x-20. (8)

The Belyĭ function f=f⁡(x,y)f=f(x,y) is then constructed as follows:

a\displaystyle a =\displaystyle= −x5−23​x4+697​x3−1031​x2−2170​x−353;\displaystyle-x^{5}-23x^{4}+697x^{3}-1031x^{2}-2170x-353;

f\displaystyle f =\displaystyle= a​y+b1728​(x−16).\displaystyle\frac{ay+b}{1728(x-16)}. (9)

(Alternatively, putting y=z−12y=z-\frac{1}{2}, x=t+13x=t+\frac{1}{3} gives

z2=t3−313​t−2501108,z^{2}=t^{3}-\frac{31}{3}t-\frac{2501}{108},

a Weierstrass form for EE. The JJ-invariant of the curve is J⁡(E)=−212​313115\displaystyle J(E)=-\frac{2^{12}31^{3}}{11^{5}}.)

Even a verification of the above result is not an easy task. We give an outline of the main steps of such a verification.

Step 0. Since the map 𝒟0​(11){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(11) has 12 directed edges, we expect its Belyĭ function to have degree 12. However, when one looks at the expression (9), this property does not jump to the eyes, to put it mildly. We have an impression that this function is rather of degree 6. The clue is that it is considered to be defined on the curve EE. Let us denote h⁡(x,y)=y2+y−x3+x2+10​x+20h(x,y)=y^{2}+y-x^{3}+x^{2}+10x+20 (see equation (8)). Expressing yy from the equation f⁡(x,y)=zf(x,y)=z and substituting the result in hh we indeed get a function of degree 12 in xx since hh contains y2y^{2}.

Step 1. In order to find critical points on the curve we must ensure that the gradients of the functions ff and hh are collinear. Hence the following determinant must be equal to zero:

|∂f∂x∂f∂y∂h∂x∂h∂y|= 0.\left|\begin{array}[]{cc}{\displaystyle\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}}&{\displaystyle\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}}\\ &\\ {\displaystyle\frac{\partial h}{\partial x}}&{\displaystyle\frac{\partial h}{\partial y}}\end{array}\right|\,=\,0.

This gives us an equation in two variables xx and yy. The second equation is h⁡(x,y)=0h(x,y)=0 since we are looking not for arbitrary points of collineation but for those which belong to EE.

Step 2. A good idea is to find a Gröbner basis for the system thus obtained, and to do it twice. Using the ‘pure lexicographic’ monomial order plex(y,x) we get as the first element of the basis a polynomial in xx; using plex(x,y) we get a polynomial in yy. Here they are:

Step 3. The roots of these two polynomials are the xx-coordinates and the yy-coordinates of the critical points of ff on EE. Two factors of degree 4, being squared, indicate that there are four critical points of multiplicity 3. We guess that they are the black vertices of our map. But is it true that the value of ff at all these points is equal to zero? We must also ‘couple’ xx- and yy-coordinates in order to show which yy correspond to which xx.

These questions are easy to answer. We solve the system f=0f=0, h=0h=0 and see that the values of xx are indeed roots of p1=x4−20​x3+62​x2+116​x+97p_{1}=x^{4}-20x^{3}+62x^{2}+116x+97, while

y=−123​(x3−16​x2+90​x+62).y=-\frac{1}{23}(x^{3}-16x^{2}+90x+62).

Beside these four solutions there is one more: (x,y)=(16,60)(x,y)=(16,60). What does it mean? There are two points on EE over x=16x=16, namely (16,60)(16,60) and (16,−61)(16,-61). Substituting y=60y=60 into the numerator of ff we get

−(x−16)​(11​x5+88​x4+2145​x3−4796​x2−8096​x−1117).-(x-16)(11x^{5}+88x^{4}+2145x^{3}-4796x^{2}-8096x-1117).

Now, the factors of degree 6 of the polynomials PP and QQ correspond to simple critical points, which are mid-points of edges. And, indeed, solving the system f=1f=1, h=0h=0, we obtain, beside the superfluous solution (16,60)(16,60), the roots of p2=x6−30​x5+243​x4−256​x3−1053​x2+654​x+7793p_{2}=x^{6}-30x^{5}+243x^{4}-256x^{3}-1053x^{2}+654x+7793, while

Step 4. Since the function ff has only one simple pole on the finite part of the curve EE, we may conclude that it also has a pole of multiplicity 11 ‘over infinity’. We might stop here. However, we prefer to make the last statement more explicit.

First of all, let us introduce the projective coordinates (X:Y:Z)(X\!:\!Y\!:\!Z), where x=X/Zx=X/Z, y=Y/Zy=Y/Z, and projectivize the equation (8) of the curve:

Figure 18 shows a geometrically correct picture of the dessin 𝒟0​(11){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(11), lifted from the torus EE to the complex plane to give a doubly periodic map. In addition to the black vertices of degree 33, the white vertices of degree 22 are also shown, as is a fundamental parallelogram for the associated lattice. The repeated copies of 𝒟0​(11){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(11) are aligned as in the right-hand map in Figure 17. However, the loop (the face of valency 11), which is obvious there, is in reality too small to be clearly visible here. Changing accuracy parameters to make this face and its incident vertices visible would create a mess elsewhere, so in this case we have to accept that nature, technology and human eyesight are incompatible. We met a similar problem earlier for 𝒟0​(13){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(13), in connection with Figures 15 and 16.

To obtain this diagram we use the substitution

y=z−12,x=t+13y=\frac{z-1}{2},\quad x=t+\frac{1}{3}

in Weierstrass normal form. Then Algorithm 7.4.7 in Cohen’s book [14], using the arithmetic-geometric mean, gives a basis

ω1=1.269209304,ω2=−0.6346046520+1.458816617​i\omega_{1}=1.269209304,\quad\omega_{2}=-0.6346046520+1.458816617i
