τ=ω2/ω1=−0.5000000000+1.149390106​i,\tau=\omega_{2}/\omega_{1}=-0.5000000000+1.149390106i,

on the left-hand vertical border of the standard fundamental region for Γ\Gamma, which is consistent with the fact that J⁡(τ)<0J(\tau)<0. To obtain the embedded graph we lift the unit interval [0,1]⊂Σ[0,1]\subset\Sigma, with black and white vertices at 00 and 11, to the curve EE via the Belyĭ function ff, and then use the standard parametrisation of EE by the Weierstrass functions, namely t=℘⁡(w)t=\wp(w) and z=℘′​(w)z=\wp^{\prime}(w) for w∈ℂw\in\mathbb{C}, to lift the resulting dessin to the plane.

11.4 The dessins 𝒟⁡(p){\mathcal{D}}(p)

The minimal regular cover of 𝒟0​(p){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(p) is a regular dessin 𝒟⁡(p){\mathcal{D}}(p) of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) with automorphism group PSL2​(p){\rm PSL}_{2}(p); for p>2p>2 it has degree p⁡(p2−1)/2p(p^{2}-1)/2 and genus (p+2)​(p−3)​(p−5)/24(p+2)(p-3)(p-5)/24, while for p=2p=2 it has degree 66 and genus 00. The underlying curves of 𝒟⁡(p){\mathcal{D}}(p) and 𝒟0​(p){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(p) are the modular curves X⁡(p)=ℍ/Γ⁡(p)¯X(p)=\overline{{\mathbb{H}}/\Gamma(p)} and X0​(p)=ℍ/Γ0​(p)¯X_{0}(p)=\overline{{\mathbb{H}}/\Gamma_{0}(p)} (hence the notation for these two dessins); here Γ⁡(p)\Gamma(p) is the principal congruence subgroup of level pp in Γ\Gamma, the kernel of the reduction mod (p):Γ→PSL2​(p)(p):\Gamma\to{\rm PSL}_{2}(p) (see [42, §6.9–10], for example), while Γ0​(p)\Gamma_{0}(p) is the inverse image in Γ\Gamma of the subgroup of PSL2​(p){\rm PSL}_{2}(p) fixing ∞\infty.

Theorem 11.1

For each prime pp the dessin 𝒟⁡(p){\mathcal{D}}(p) is the only regular dessin of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) with automorphism group G=PSL2​(p)G={\rm PSL}_{2}(p), and 𝒟0​(p){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(p) is the only dessin of degree p+1p+1 and type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) with monodromy group GG.

To prove the uniqueness of 𝒟⁡(p){\mathcal{D}}(p) it is sufficient to show that GG has, up to automorphisms, only one generating triple (x,y,z)(x,y,z) of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p). The elements z∈Gz\in G of order pp are all equivalent under automorphisms, while the elements of order 33 and 22 are those with traces ±1\pm 1 and 00. We may therefore assume that

y=±(abc−a)andz=±(1011),so thaty​z=±(a+bbc−a−a).y=\pm\left(\,\begin{array}[]{cc}a&b\\ c&-a\\ \end{array}\right)\quad\hbox{and}\quad z=\pm\left(\,\begin{array}[]{cc}1&0\\ 1&1\\ \end{array}\right),\quad\hbox{so that}\quad yz=\pm\left(\,\begin{array}[]{cc}a+b&b\\ c-a&-a\\ \end{array}\right).

Since we require y​z=x−1yz=x^{-1} to have order 33 we must have b=±1b=\pm 1, and without loss of generality we can take b=1b=1. Since dety=1\det y=1 we have c=−a2−1c=-a^{2}-1, giving a 11-parameter set of solutions

y=ya=±(a1−a2−1−a)(a∈𝔽p).y=y_{a}=\pm\left(\,\begin{array}[]{cc}a&1\\ -a^{2}-1&-a\\ \end{array}\right)\quad(a\in{\mathbb{F}}_{p}).

Now conjugating the triple (x,y,z)(x,y,z) with ziz^{i} fixes zz and replaces y=yay=y_{a} with ya+iy_{a+i}, so all such triples are equivalent under automorphisms, as required. One could also prove this by using the Frobenius triple-counting formula (2), as in Example 4.1 for p=11p=11 (see [44, §5.5] for the character table of GG); this is easy if p≡±5p\equiv\pm 5 mod (12)(12) since in this case only one nonprincipal irreducible character, of degree pp, appears in the character sum, but if p≡±1p\equiv\pm 1 mod (12)(12) then other characters appear and some work with algebraic numbers is required. Since GG has a unique conjugacy class of subgroups of index p+1p+1, namely the stabilisers of points in ℙ1​(𝔽p){\mathbb{P}}^{1}({\mathbb{F}}_{p}), it follows that 𝒟0​(p){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(p) is the only dessin of degree p+1p+1 and type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) with monodromy group GG.

12 Dessins of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) and degree p+1p+1

Having considered the dessins 𝒟0​(p){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(p) in the preceding section, we will now consider arbitrary dessins of their type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) and degree p+1p+1. The monodromy group GG of such a dessin 𝒟\mathcal{D} is a transitive permutation group of degree p+1p+1, and since it contains a pp-cycle zz it is doubly transitive, and hence primitive. As before, if p>3p>3, as we shall assume, GG is perfect. The finite primitive groups containing a cycle with one fixed point were determined by Müller in [65, Theorem 6.2], and as a corollary we have:

Theorem 12.1

The perfect permutation groups of degree p+1p+1 (pp prime), containing a pp-cycle, are the following:

  • (a)

    Ap+1{\rm A}_{p+1} for primes p≥5p\geq 5,

  • (b)

    PSL2​(p){\rm PSL}_{2}(p) for primes p≥5p\geq 5,

  • (c)

    affine groups AGLn​(2){\rm AGL}_{n}(2)  for Mersenne primes p=2n−1≥5p=2^{n}-1\geq 5,

  • (d)

    Mathieu groups M11{\rm M}_{11}  and M12{\rm M}_{12}  for p=11p=11 and M24{\rm M}_{24}  for p=23p=23,

all except M11{\rm M}_{11} (see below) in their natural representations.

We will consider these groups in turn, together with their analogues for p<5p<5, to see which of them can serve as monodromy groups of dessins of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p). The results will be summarized in Theorem 12.5. It is convenient to deal with the simplest cases (b) and (d) first, and to treat the alternating groups last.

The groups PSL2​(p){\rm PSL}_{2}(p) in Theorem 12.1(b) arise as monodromy groups in this context for all primes pp, each of them associated with a unique dessin, the modular dessin 𝒟0​(p){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(p) (see Theorem 11.1).

In (d), although M11{\rm M}_{11} has a permutation representation of degree 1212, on the cosets of a subgroup PSL2​(11){\rm PSL}_{2}(11), we have seen in Example 4.2 that it is not a quotient of Δ⁡(3,2,11)\Delta(3,2,11), since all triples of this type in M11{\rm M}_{11} generate not M11{\rm M}_{11} but its subgroup PSL2​(11){\rm PSL}_{2}(11); thus it does not arise as a monodromy group in this context.

The group G=M12G={\rm M}_{12} in (d) has two representations of degree 1212, on the cosets of two conjugacy classes of subgroups isomorphic to M11{\rm M}_{11}, transposed by Out​G{\rm Out}\,G. It is the monodromy group of two chiral pairs of planar dessins of type (3,2,11)(3,2,11) and degree 1212. One dessin from each pair is shown in Figure 19: the dessin on the left has passport (33​13,26,111​11)(3^{3}1^{3},2^{6},11^{1}1^{1}), with 𝒳=3​A{\mathcal{X}}=3A and 𝒴=2​A{\mathcal{Y}}=2A, while that on the right has passport (34,24​14,111​11)(3^{4},2^{4}1^{4},11^{1}1^{1}), with 𝒳=3​B{\mathcal{X}}=3B and 𝒴=2​B{\mathcal{Y}}=2B. Their regular covers are a pair of dessins of type (3,2,11)(3,2,11) and genus 36013601. There are no other dessins of this type and degree with monodromy group G=M12G={\rm M}_{12}: taking 𝒳=3​B{\mathcal{X}}=3B and 𝒴=2​A{\mathcal{Y}}=2A, or 𝒳=3​A{\mathcal{X}}=3A and 𝒴=2​B{\mathcal{Y}}=2B yields two more orbits of Aut​G{\rm Aut}\,G on triples, but these generate transitive or intransitive subgroups isomorphic to PSL2​(11){\rm PSL}_{2}(11). The dessin corresponding to these transitive subgroups has already been shown in Figures 17 and 18, while the intransitive subgroups, with orbits of length 1111 and 11, are the monodromy groups of the dessins ℳ1{\mathcal{M}}_{1} and ℳ¯1\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1} of degree 1111 in Figures 1, 2 and 3.

For p=23p=23, the group M24{\rm M}_{24} in (d), found by Mathieu [63] in 1873, is the monodromy group of two chiral pairs of planar dessins, with passports (36​16,212,231​11)(3^{6}1^{6},2^{12},23^{1}1^{1}) and (38,28​18,231​11)(3^{8},2^{8}1^{8},23^{1}1^{1}): see orbits 24.2 and 24.1 in [1, pp. 129–130]. For the first pair 𝒳=3​A\mathcal{X}=3A, 𝒴=2​B\mathcal{Y}=2B and 𝒵=23​A\mathcal{Z}=23A or 23​B23B, while for the second pair 𝒳=3​B\mathcal{X}=3B, 𝒴=2​A\mathcal{Y}=2A and 𝒵=23​A\mathcal{Z}=23A or 23​B23B. A member of each pair is shown in Figure 20. Unlike in the case of M12{\rm M}_{12}, there is a single permutation representation of degree p+1p+1 (the natural representation, on the cosets of a subgroup M23{\rm M}_{23}), and there is no outer automorphism transposing the two mutually inverse conjugacy classes of elements of order pp.

We now consider case (c) of Theorem 12.1, the affine groups AGLn​(2){\rm AGL}_{n}(2), where nn is prime and pp is a Mersenne prime 2n−12^{n}-1. The case p=3p=3 does not arise since AGL2​(2)≅S4{\rm AGL}_{2}(2)\cong{\rm S}_{4}, so this group is not a quotient of Δ⁡(3,2,2)≅S3\Delta(3,2,2)\cong{\rm S}_{3}. For p=7p=7 the only dessin of type (3,2,7)(3,2,7) and degree 88 is 𝒟0​(7){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(7), with monodromy group PSL2​(7){\rm PSL}_{2}(7), so AGL3​(2){\rm AGL}_{3}(2) does not arise. (Note that the Hurwitz group of genus 1717 is a nonsplit extension of V8{\rm V}_{8} by GL3​(2){\rm GL}_{3}(2), not isomorphic to AGL3​(2){\rm AGL}_{3}(2), and it has no transitive permutation representation of degree 88; see [45] for details.) On the other hand, for p=31p=31 orbit 32.1 in [1, pp. 134–135] consists of six planar dessins of type (3,2,31)(3,2,31) and degree 3232 with monodromy group ASL5​(2)=AGL5​(2){\rm ASL}_{5}(2)={\rm AGL}_{5}(2). These are shown in Section 14, Figure 28.

Theorem 12.2

For each Mersenne prime p=2n−1>7p=2^{n}-1>7 there are dessins of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) and degree p+1p+1 with passport (3(p−1)/3​12,2(p+1)/2,p1​11)(3^{(p-1)/3}1^{2},2^{(p+1)/2},p^{1}1^{1}), genus (p+5)/12(p+5)/12 and monodromy group AGLn​(2){\rm AGL}_{n}(2).

Proof. We will use the fact that G:=AGLn​(2)G:={\rm AGL}_{n}(2) is a semidirect product of its translation subgroup T≅(C2)nT\cong({\rm C}_{2})^{n} by G0:=GLn​(2)G_{0}:={\rm GL}_{n}(2), the stabiliser of 00. Let (x,y,z)(x,y,z) be a generating triple for GLn​(2){\rm GL}_{n}(2) of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p), chosen as in the proof of Theorem 10.11 by taking r=s=1r=s=1, so that α=1\alpha=1 and β=(n+1)/2\beta=(n+1)/2. Now let u=x​au=xa, v=y​bv=yb and w=z​cw=zc, where a,b,c∈Ta,b,c\in T. We will try to choose a,ba,b and cc so that (u,v,w)(u,v,w) is a generating triple for GG of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p).

Since x3=1x^{3}=1 we have

u3=(x​a)3=x3​ax2​ax​a=ax2+x+1,u^{3}=(xa)^{3}=x^{3}a^{x^{2}}a^{x}a=a^{x^{2}+x+1},

so u3=1u^{3}=1 if and only if a∈Tx:=ker⁡(x2+x+1)a\in T_{x}:=\ker(x^{2}+x+1). (Here we regard x2+x+1x^{2}+x+1 as a linear transformation of the vector space TT over 𝔽2{\mathbb{F}}_{2}.) Similarly v2=1v^{2}=1 if and only if b∈Ty:=ker⁡(y+1)b\in T_{y}:=\ker(y+1), and wp=1w^{p}=1 if and only if c∈Tz:=ker⁡(zp−1+zp−2+⋯+z+1)c\in T_{z}:=\ker(z^{p-1}+z^{p-2}+\cdots+z+1). Also

u​v​w=x​a.y​b.z​c=x​y​ay​z​bz​c=x​y​z​ay​z​bz​c=ay​z​bz​c,uvw=xa.yb.zc=xya^{y}zb^{z}c=xyza^{yz}b^{z}c=a^{yz}b^{z}c,

so u​v​w=1uvw=1 if and only if ay​z​bz​c=1a^{yz}b^{z}c=1.

Since zz is a Singer cycle in G0G_{0}, Tz=TT_{z}=T and hence the condition on cc is vacuous, whereas the Jordan forms for xx and yy used in the proof of Theorem 10.11 show that the subspaces TxT_{x} and TyT_{y} have dimensions n−1n-1 and (n+1)/2(n+1)/2. Within these subspaces one can choose aa and bb arbitrarily, and then define c=ay​z​bzc=a^{yz}b^{z}, so that av​y​z​bz​c=1a^{vyz}b^{z}c=1 and hence (u,v,w)(u,v,w) is a triple of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p).

The cycle structures of uu, vv and ww can be found as follows. One can regard AGLn​(2){\rm AGL}_{n}(2) as acting naturally on TT, with elements of TT and GLn​(2){\rm GL}_{n}(2) acting by translations and by linear transformations. The element u=x​au=xa acts on TT by t↦tx​at\mapsto t^{x}a, so it fixes an element t∈Tt\in T if and only if a=t⁡(1−x)a=t(1-x), using additive notation for the vector space TT. Now the Jordan form for xx shows that T⁡(1−x)=TxT(1-x)=T_{x}, so for every choice of a∈Txa\in T_{x} there are |ker⁡(1−x)|=2|\ker(1-x)|=2 fixed points t∈Tt\in T for uu. Since uu has order 33 it has (p−1)/3(p-1)/3 cycles of length 33. In the case of vv the Jordan form for yy shows that T⁡(1−y)T(1-y) is a subspace of codimension 11 in TyT_{y}, so by choosing b∈Ty∖T⁡(1−y)b\in T_{y}\setminus T(1-y) we can ensure that vv has no fixed points, and therefore consists of (p+1)/2(p+1)/2 transpositions. Since ww has order pp it has cycle structure p1​11p^{1}1^{1}.

Now let us define H:=⟨u,v,w⟩≤GH:=\langle u,v,w\rangle\leq G. We will prove that if p>7p>7 then H=GH=G. Factoring out TT maps HH onto ⟨x,y,z⟩=G0\langle x,y,z\rangle=G_{0}, so H​T=GHT=G. If HH contains a non-identity translation t∈Tt\in T then since HH contains ww it contains all the non-identity translations twt^{w}, so H≥TH\geq T and hence H=GH=G, as required.

We may therefore assume, for a contradiction, that H∩T=1H\cap T=1, so that HH is a complement for TT in GG. Since the first cohomology group H1​(GLn​(2),T)H^{1}({\rm GL}_{n}(2),T) for GLn​(2){\rm GL}_{n}(2) on its natural module TT is trivial for all n>3n>3 (see [4]) there is a single conjugacy class of such complements, so HH is a point-stabiliser in the natural action of GG. This contradicts the fact that vv has no fixed points, by our choice of the translation bb.

Thus (u,v,w)(u,v,w) is a generating triple for GG, so it corresponds to a dessin of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) and degree p+1p+1 with monodromy group GG. Its genus follows from its passport, determined above. □\square

The above proof fails in the case p=7p=7 since |H1​(GL3​(2),T)|=2|H^{1}({\rm GL}_{3}(2),T)|=2 (see [4]), so that there are two conjugacy classes of complements for TT in AGL3​(2){\rm AGL}_{3}(2), consisting of the point-stabilisers and of subgroups acting transitively on TT as PSL2​(7){\rm PSL}_{2}(7); in this case every triple of type (3,2,7)(3,2,7) generates a complement. (The fact that all complements are isomorphic to G/TG/T provides a simple proof that GL3​(2)≅PSL2​(7){\rm GL}_{3}(2)\cong{\rm PSL}_{2}(7).)

Example 12.3

Taking n=5n=5 we obtain a dessin of type (3,2,31)(3,2,31), degree 3232 and genus 33, with passport (310​12,216,311​11)(3^{10}1^{2},2^{16},31^{1}1^{1}). This should not be confused with the Galois orbit 32.1 of six planar dessins with the same type, degree and monodromy group in [1]: these have passport (310​12,212​18,311​11)(3^{10}1^{2},2^{12}1^{8},31^{1}1^{1}), and they correspond to taking b∈T⁡(1−y)b\in T(1-y), so that vv fixes |ker⁡(1−y)|=8|\ker(1-y)|=8 points (see Subsection 14.6).

Finally, we consider the alternating groups Ap+1{\rm A}_{p+1}, in case (a) of Theorem 12.1, as monodromy groups.

Theorem 12.4

The alternating group Ap+1{\rm A}_{p+1}, pp prime, is the monodromy group of a dessin of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) and degree p+1p+1 if and only if p=3p=3 or p≥11p\geq 11.

Proof. For p=2,5p=2,5 or 77 the triangle group Δ⁡(3,2,p)\Delta(3,2,p) does not map onto Ap+1{\rm A}_{p+1}: this is obvious if p=2p=2 or 55, and for p=7p=7 it is well known that A8{\rm A}_{8} is not a Hurwitz group: the triples of type (3,2,7)(3,2,7) in this group all generate proper subgroups isomorphic to PSL2​(7){\rm PSL}_{2}(7). On the other hand, A4{\rm A}_{4} is the monodromy group of the dessin of type (3,2,3)(3,2,3) and degree 44 on the left in Figure 21, the quotient of the tetrahedron {3,3}\{3,3\} by C3{\rm C}_{3}. (Note that A4{\rm A}_{4} is isomorphic to PSL2​(3){\rm PSL}_{2}(3) in case (b).)

For p=11p=11 and 1313 it is sufficient by Theorem 12.1 to note that the dessins of degree 1212 and 1414 in Figure 21 are not isomorphic to the unique dessins 𝒟0​(p){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(p) with monodromy group PSL2​(p){\rm PSL}_{2}(p) shown in Figures 17 and 13.

Finally, let p≥17p\geq 17. If p≡2p\equiv 2 mod (3)(3), say p=3​k+2p=3k+2 for some k≥5k\geq 5, consider the dessin 𝒟\mathcal{D} in Figure 22, where there are kk vertices of degree 33, so that the degree of 𝒟\mathcal{D} is p+1p+1 and its passport is (3k​13,2k+3​1k−3,p1​11)(3^{k}1^{3},2^{k+3}1^{k-3},p^{1}1^{1}). The monodromy group of 𝒟\mathcal{D} cannot be PSL2​(p){\rm PSL}_{2}(p) since a non-identity element of that group has at most two fixed points, whereas xx has three; similarly it cannot be AGLn​(2){\rm AGL}_{n}(2) for any nn since the fixed point set of any element of that group is either empty or an affine subspace of order 2d2^{d} for some dd; finally, it cannot be a Mathieu group since 𝒟\mathcal{D} is not isomorphic to any of the dessins in Figures 19 or 20 or their mirror images, so it must be Ap+1{\rm A}_{p+1}.

If p≡1p\equiv 1 mod (3)(3), say p=3​k+4p=3k+4 for some k≥5k\geq 5, one can apply a similar argument to the dessin 𝒟′{\mathcal{D}}^{\prime} obtained by adding two vertices of valency 11 to the rightmost free edges of 𝒟\mathcal{D}, so that the passport is (3k​15,2k+5​1k−5,p1​11)(3^{k}1^{5},2^{k+5}1^{k-5},p^{1}1^{1}). □\square

By reflecting an arbitrary subset of the free edges of 𝒟\mathcal{D} or 𝒟′{\mathcal{D}}^{\prime} one obtains exponentially many dessins of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) and degree p+1p+1 with monodromy group Ap+1{\rm A}_{p+1} as p→∞p\to\infty.

We summarise the results of the last two sections as follows:

Theorem 12.5

Suppose that pp is a prime such that there is a dessin of type (3,2,p)(3,2,p) and degree p+1p+1 with monodromy group GG. Then one of the following holds:

  • (a)

    G=Ap+1G={\rm A}_{p+1}, with p=3p=3 or p≥11p\geq 11,

  • (b)

    G=PSL2​(p)G={\rm PSL}_{2}(p),

  • (c)

    G=AGLn​(2)G={\rm AGL}_{n}(2) for some Mersenne prime p=2n−1≥31p=2^{n}-1\geq 31,

  • (d)

    G=M12G={\rm M}_{12} with p=11p=11 or G=M24G={\rm M}_{24} with p=23p=23,

each in its natural representation. In case (a) there are exponentially many dessins as p→∞p\to\infty, even if we restrict to planar dessins. In case (b) there is a single dessin 𝒟0​(p){\mathcal{D}}_{0}(p) for each prime pp. In case (c) there is at least one dessin for each Mersenne prime pp. In case (d) there are two chiral pairs for each of the two groups GG.

13 The road not taken

The starting point for Klein’s work in [51], and hence for our investigation in this paper, was the embedding of the icosahedral group A5{\rm A}_{5} in PSL2​(11){\rm PSL}_{2}(11). This is the third and most complicated of the three instances, known already to Galois, of PSL2​(p){\rm PSL}_{2}(p) having a subgroup of index pp; the first two, for p=5p=5 and 77, each became the subject of a deservedly famous book (respectively [52] and [55]), and one could easily imagine (though not so easily write) an analogue for p=11p=11. In this final section we will briefly sketch a line of research which might form the basis of a chapter in such a text; the road it takes is almost completely disjoint from that we have followed in the present paper; however, there is an intriguing moment when we catch a brief glimpse of the road starting with Klein’s paper [50] concerning the case p=7p=7.

There are a number of mathematical objects and phenomena closely related to the embedding (or more precisely the embeddings) of A5{\rm A}_{5} in the group L=PSL2​(11)L={\rm PSL}_{2}(11). A good example is the non-orientable regular abstract polytope {3,5,3}55{}_{5}\{3,5,3\}_{5}, the hendecachoron or 1111-cell independently discovered by Grünbaum [36] and Coxeter [18] (see also [19, 21] for this example, and [60] for the general theory of abstract polytopes).

Let Γ\Gamma denote the string Coxeter group with Schläfli symbol {3,5,3}\{3,5,3\}, represented by the Coxeter diagram in Figure 23. This group has generators Ri​(i=0,…,3)R_{i}\;(i=0,\ldots,3) and defining relations

Ri2=(R0​R1)3=(R1​R2)5=(R2​R3)3=1,(Ri​Rj)2=1​whenever​|i−j|≥2;R_{i}^{2}=(R_{0}R_{1})^{3}=(R_{1}R_{2})^{5}=(R_{2}R_{3})^{3}=1,\quad(R_{i}R_{j})^{2}=1\;\hbox{whenever}\;|i-j|\geq 2;

it acts as a group of isometries of hyperbolic 33-space ℍ3{\mathbb{H}}^{3}, generated by reflections RiR_{i} in the sides of a tetrahedron T⊂ℍ3T\subset{\mathbb{H}}^{3} with appropriate dihedral angles. As shown in [43] there is a unique normal subgroup NN of Γ\Gamma such that Γ/N≅L\Gamma/N\cong L. This is the normal closure of the elements (R0​R1​R2)5(R_{0}R_{1}R_{2})^{5} and (R1​R2​R3)5(R_{1}R_{2}R_{3})^{5}, so that putting these equal to 11 in Γ\Gamma gives a presentation for LL.

The quotient ℍ3/N{\mathbb{H}}^{3}/N is a compact non-orientable hyperbolic 33-orbifold 𝒩\mathcal{N}, with a tessellation 𝒯\mathcal{T} by |L|=660|L|=660 tetrahedra, induced from the tessellation of ℍ3{\mathbb{H}}^{3} by the images of TT under Γ\Gamma. These tetrahedra can be partitioned into eleven sets of 6060, giving a tessellation ℐ\mathcal{I} of 𝒩\mathcal{N} by eleven hemi-icosahedra {3,5}5\{3,5\}_{5} (antipodal quotients of icosahedra {3,5}\{3,5\} formed by identifying edges five steps apart along Petrie paths), which has 𝒯\mathcal{T} as its barycentric subdivision. Similarly ℐ\mathcal{I} has eleven vertices, each having as its vertex figure a hemi-dodecahedron {5,3}5\{5,3\}_{5} formed in the same way from a dodecahedron {5,3}\{5,3\}. This tessellation ℐ\mathcal{I} is a realisation of Coxeter’s non-orientable regular polytope {3,5,3}55{}_{5}\{3,5,3\}_{5}, with the subscripts indicating these identifications, and also the corresponding extra defining relations for LL. It has automorphism group LL, with the stabilisers of cells and of vertices forming the two conjugacy classes of subgroups H≅A5H\cong{\rm A}_{5} in LL, represented by the images of the subgroups ⟨R0,R1,R2⟩≅⟨R1,R2,R3⟩≅Δ⁡[3,2,5]≅A5×C2\langle R_{0},R_{1},R_{2}\rangle\cong\langle R_{1},R_{2},R_{3}\rangle\cong\Delta[3,2,5]\cong{\rm A}_{5}\times{\rm C}_{2} of Γ\Gamma. Notice that NN is not torsion-free (it contains the central involution of each of these subgroups), so 𝒩\mathcal{N} is not a manifold.

The normaliser Ω\Omega of Γ\Gamma in the isometry group of ℍ3{\mathbb{H}}^{3} is a semidirect product of Γ\Gamma by a group C2{\rm C}_{2} induced by the graph automorphism Ri↦R3−iR_{i}\mapsto R_{3-i} of Γ\Gamma; this leaves NN invariant, with Ω/N≅PGL2​(11)\Omega/N\cong{\rm PGL}_{2}(11), and acts as a self-duality of ℐ\mathcal{I}, transposing vertices and cells, and edges and faces. The group Ω\Omega plays a similar role in the theory of compact 33-manifolds to that played by the triangle groups Δ⁡(3,2,7)\Delta(3,2,7) and Δ⁡[3,2,7]\Delta[3,2,7] for Riemann and Klein surfaces: specifically, as shown by Gehring, Marshall and Martin [29, 61], Ω\Omega has the least covolume among all cocompact discontinuous groups of isometries of ℍ3{\mathbb{H}}^{3}. It follows that the torsion-free normal subgroups KK of finite index in Ω\Omega uniformise the compact hyperbolic 33-manifolds which maximise the number of automorphisms, namely |Ω/K||\Omega/K|, per unit of volume. As such, these manifolds and automorphism groups are the 33-dimensional analogues of the Hurwitz curves and groups in dimension 22. As shown in [43], among such subgroups KK that of least index is K=N∩Ω+K=N\cap\Omega^{+}, where Ω+\Omega^{+} is the orientation-preserving subgroup of index 22 in Ω\Omega. The corresponding orientable manifold 𝒦=ℍ3/K{\mathcal{K}}={\mathbb{H}}^{3}/K, a double covering of the orbifold 𝒩\mathcal{N}, has isometry group Ω/K≅PGL2​(11)×C2\Omega/K\cong{\rm PGL}_{2}(11)\times{\rm C}_{2}, with orientation-preserving subgroup Ω+/K≅PGL2​(11)\Omega^{+}/K\cong{\rm PGL}_{2}(11); the subgroup Γ/K≅L×C2\Gamma/K\cong L\times{\rm C}_{2} preserves a tessellation of 𝒦\mathcal{K} by eleven icosahedra, with the two conjugacy classes of icosahedral subgroups A5×C2{\rm A}_{5}\times{\rm C}_{2} stabilising the cells and vertices, and transposed in Ω/K\Omega/K by duality. By the minimality of their volumes, 𝒦\mathcal{K} and 𝒩\mathcal{N} can be regarded as 33-dimensional analogues of Klein’s quartic curve [50], the smallest Riemann surface attaining the Hurwitz bound on the number of automorphisms per unit of area (see [55] for connections with PSL2​(7){\rm PSL}_{2}(7) and [50]). Figure 24 shows the relevant subgroups of Ω\Omega, together with their quotients by KK, that is, the finite groups of isometries they induce on 𝒦\mathcal{K}.

Remark 14.2

The next Fermat prime, after 17, is 257. Let us give a cursory glance at the group PSL2​(256){\rm PSL}_{2}(256). Their passport is (385​12,2128​11,2571)(3^{85}1^{2},2^{128}1^{1},257^{1}), and their genus is g=21g=21, in accordance with Theorem 10.1. The next candidate for our series of examples would be the group PSL7​(2){\rm PSL}_{7}(2) of degree 127. Since we don’t see any particular interest in writing explicitly the generating permutations of that large degree, we stop here.
